paper.text: Four schemata axiomatize Łukasiewicz logic. Reading $\psi\dot-\varphi$ as "$\psi$ is at most $\varphi$": (A1) $\varphi\dot-\psi$ is at most $\varphi$; (A2) $(\chi\dot-\varphi)\dot-(\chi\dot-\psi)$ is at most $\psi\dot-\varphi$; (A3) $\varphi\dot-(\varphi\dot-\psi)$ is at most $\psi\dot-(\psi\dot-\varphi)$ (both express the minimum); (A4) $\varphi\dot-\psi$ is at most $\neg\psi\dot-\neg\varphi$ (contraposition).

Group1Axioms/LukPropForm/IsAxiom.summary: The axiom schemata (A1)–(A4) as an inductive predicate on Łukasiewicz formulae.
Group1Axioms/LukPropForm/IsAxiom.english:
**Definition** (`LukPropForm.IsAxiom`). A formula is an axiom if it is an instance, for some formulae $\varphi,\psi,\chi$, of
(A1) $(\varphi\dot-\psi)\dot-\varphi$,
(A2) $((\chi\dot-\varphi)\dot-(\chi\dot-\psi))\dot-(\psi\dot-\varphi)$,
(A3) $(\varphi\dot-(\varphi\dot-\psi))\dot-(\psi\dot-(\psi\dot-\varphi))$, or
(A4) $(\varphi\dot-\psi)\dot-(\neg\psi\dot-\neg\varphi)$.

Group1Axioms/LukPropForm/IterSub.title: Iterated truncated subtraction of Łukasiewicz formulae

paper.text: For a natural number $n$, $\psi\dot-n\varphi$ abbreviates subtracting $\varphi$ from $\psi$ $n$ times in succession, starting from $\psi$ itself when $n=0$.

Group1Axioms/LukPropForm/Provable.title: Provability and consistency in Łukasiewicz logic

paper.text: Proofs use modus ponens as the only rule: from $\varphi$ and $\psi\dot-\varphi$ infer $\psi$. $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$ means that some finite derivation from axioms and members of $\Sigma$ ends in $\varphi$. A set is inconsistent if it proves every formula, and consistent otherwise.

Group1Axioms/LukPropForm/Provable.summary: The provability relation $\Sigma\vdash^{\mathrm L}\varphi$ as the least set containing the axioms and $\Sigma$ and closed under modus ponens, and consistency as "some formula is unprovable".
Group1Axioms/LukPropForm/Provable.english:
**Definition** (`LukPropForm.Provable`). $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$ is generated by three rules: every axiom is provable; every member of $\Sigma$ is provable; and if $\varphi$ and $\psi\dot-\varphi$ are provable then so is $\psi$ (modus ponens). This inductive definition is equivalent to the paper's finite derivations: a formula is provable exactly when it is the last line of a finite sequence each of whose lines is an axiom, a hypothesis, or follows from two earlier lines by modus ponens.

**Definition** (`Consistent`). $\Sigma$ is consistent if there is a formula $\varphi$ with $\Sigma\nvdash\varphi$.

Group2Axioms/BaseAxiomSchema.title: The axiom schemata (A1)–(A9)

paper.text: The quantifier schemata imitate classical ones: (A7) $\sup$ distributes over $\dot-$ in the sense that $(\sup_x\psi\dot-\sup_x\varphi)\dot-\sup_x(\psi\dot-\varphi)$ is an axiom; (A8) a correct instance $\varphi[t/x]$ is below $\sup_x\varphi$; and (A9) $\sup_x\varphi$ is below $\varphi$ when $x$ is not free in $\varphi$.
The propositional schemata (A1)–(A6) of §3 are taken over verbatim, now ranging over first-order formulae.

Group2Axioms/BaseAxiomSchema.summary: The first-order axiom schemata for an arbitrary signature: (A1)–(A6) at first-order formulae, plus (A7)–(A9).

Group2Axioms/ConsistentQ.title: Consistency

paper.text: A set of formulae is inconsistent if it proves every formula, and consistent otherwise.

Group2Axioms/ConsistentQ.summary: First-order consistency, with and without a metric.
Group2Axioms/ConsistentQ.english: **Definition.** $\Gamma$ is consistent iff some formula is not provable from $\Gamma$ (for the metric version, not provable with (A1)–(A14)).

Group2Axioms/FormulaGenList.title: Generalizations

paper.text: A generalization of $\psi$ is any formula $\sup_{x_1}\cdots\sup_{x_n}\psi$ with $n\ge0$; in particular $\psi$ is a generalization of itself. Every generalization of an axiom instance is itself an axiom.

Group2Axioms/FormulaGenList.english: **Definition** (`genList`). For a list $x_1,\dots,x_n$: the empty list gives $\psi$, and $x::xs$ gives $\sup_x(\mathrm{gen}_{xs}\psi)$.

Group2Axioms/MetricAxiomSchema.title: The metric axiom schemata (A10)–(A14)

paper.text: For a signature with a metric add: (A10)–(A12) say that $d$ is a pseudo-metric ($dxx$, $dxy\dot-dyx$, $(dxz\dot-dxy)\dot-dyz$). (A13) and (A14) encode the moduli: for a dyadic $q$ below $\delta_{s,i}(\epsilon)$ and a dyadic $r$ above $\epsilon$, the formula $(q\dot-dzw)\wedge(\text{change of }s\text{ in argument }i\text{ when }z\text{ is replaced by }w\ \dot-\ r)$ is an axiom. Informally, whenever $d(z,w)<q$, the first conjunct is positive, so the second must vanish and the change is at most $r$; letting $r\downarrow\epsilon$ recovers the modulus.

Group2Axioms/MetricAxiomSchema.summary: (A1)–(A9) together with (A10)–(A14) for a metric signature.
Group2Axioms/MetricAxiomSchema.english:
**Definition** (`MetricAxiomSchema`). Every base instance is an instance, and in addition, for variables $x,y,z,w$, a tuple of variables $\bar v$, and $\bar v[i\mapsto z]$ the tuple with the $i$-th entry replaced:
(A10) $d(x,x)$; (A11) $d(x,y)\dot-d(y,x)$; (A12) $(d(x,z)\dot-d(x,y))\dot-d(y,z)$;
(A13) for a function symbol $f$, an index $i$, a real $\epsilon\in(0,1]$ and dyadic codes $r,q$ with $\epsilon<r$ and $q<\delta_{f,i}(\epsilon)$:
$\big(q\dot-d(z,w)\big)\wedge\big(d(f(\bar v[i\mapsto z]),f(\bar v[i\mapsto w]))\dot-r\big)$;
(A14) for a relation symbol $P$ and the same side conditions:
$\big(q\dot-d(z,w)\big)\wedge\big((P(\bar v[i\mapsto z])\dot-P(\bar v[i\mapsto w]))\dot-r\big)$.

*Remark.* The arguments other than the $i$-th are variables, as in the paper's $f\bar xz\bar y$.

Group2Axioms/ProvableMetricQ.title: Provability with a metric

paper.text: With a metric, the axioms are the generalizations of instances of (A1)–(A14).

Group2Axioms/ProvableMetricQ.english: **Definition** (`ProvableMetricQ`). As `ProvableQ`, but the axioms are generalizations of instances of (A1)–(A14).

Group2Axioms/ProvableQ.title: Provability without a metric

paper.text: $\Gamma\vdash_Q\varphi$ means $\varphi$ has a deduction from $\Gamma$ whose axioms are generalizations of instances of the schemata, with modus ponens as the only rule.

Group2Axioms/ProvableQ.english: **Definition** (`ProvableQ`). The least relation such that every generalization of an instance of (A1)–(A9) is provable, every member of $\Gamma$ is provable, and if $\varphi$ and $\psi\dot-\varphi$ are provable then so is $\psi$ (modus ponens: $\psi\dot-\varphi$ says "$\varphi\to\psi$").

Group2Axioms/SoundnessMetric.title: Soundness with a metric

paper.text: For a signature with a metric, soundness holds with respect to pre-structures and to complete structures; the validity of (A10)–(A14) is exactly the discussion following (A14): the pseudo-metric axioms hold because $d$ is a pseudo-metric, and (A13)–(A14) hold because the symbols obey their moduli.

Group2Axioms/SoundnessMetric.summary: Validity of (A10)–(A14) in metric pre-structures and the full Theorem 7.2 for signatures with a metric.
Group2Axioms/SoundnessMetric.english:
**Lemma** (`metricAxiom_eval_zero`). Every instance of (A1)–(A14) has value $0$ in every metric pre-structure under every assignment.

*Proof.* (A1)–(A9) as before. (A10)–(A12) are $d(x,x)=0$, symmetry and the triangle inequality. For (A13): write $D=d(z,w)$ and $E=d(f(\dots z\dots),f(\dots w\dots))$; the value is $\min(q\dot-D,\ E\dot-r)$. If $D<q$, then $D<q<\delta_{f,i}(\epsilon)$, so by the modulus $E\le\epsilon<r$ and the second term is $0$; otherwise the first term is $0$. (A14) is the same with the truncated difference of relation values.

**Theorem** (`soundness_metric_pre`, `soundness_metric`). If $\Gamma\vdash_Q\varphi$ with the metric axioms, then $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ over metric pre-structures and hence $\Gamma\models_{QC}\varphi$ over complete structures.

**Theorem** (`soundness_metric_full`, Theorem 7.2). (i) $\Gamma\vdash_Q\varphi$ implies $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ and $\Gamma\models_{QC}\varphi$; (ii) if $\Gamma$ is satisfiable, or completely satisfiable, then $\Gamma$ is consistent.

*Proof.* (i) by induction on derivations as before. (ii): in a model the formula $1$ has value $1$, so it is not provable.

Group2Axioms/SoundnessPre.title: Soundness without a metric

paper.text: Soundness: provable consequences are semantic consequences, and a satisfiable set is consistent. It suffices that every axiom is valid: (A1)–(A6) by the propositional facts, (A7)–(A9) by the substitution results of §6.

Group2Axioms/SoundnessPre.summary: Every generalization of an (A1)–(A9) instance is valid; hence $\Gamma\vdash_Q\varphi\Rightarrow\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$, and satisfiable sets are consistent.
Group2Axioms/SoundnessPre.english:
**Lemma** (`eval_genList_eq_zero`). If $\psi$ has value $0$ under every assignment in $\mathfrak M$, so does every generalization of $\psi$.

*Proof.* Induction on the list: a supremum of zeros is zero.

**Lemma** (`baseAxiom_eval_zero`). Every instance of (A1)–(A9) has value $0$ in every pre-structure under every assignment.

*Proof.* (A1)–(A6) are real inequalities about $\dot-$, $1-x$ and $x/2$ on $[0,1]$, checked by cases. (A7): for every $a$, $\psi(a)\le(\psi(a)\dot-\varphi(a))+\varphi(a)\le\sup(\psi\dot-\varphi)+\sup\varphi$, so $\sup\psi\dot-\sup\varphi\le\sup(\psi\dot-\varphi)$. (A8): by the Substitution Lemma, $\varphi[t/x]$ has the value of $\varphi$ at $\sigma^a_x$ for $a=t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}$, which is at most the supremum. (A9): if $x$ is not free, every $\sigma^a_x$ gives the same value as $\sigma$, so the supremum equals that value.

**Theorem** (`soundness_pre`, Theorem 7.2(i)). If $\Gamma\vdash_Q\varphi$ then $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ (over pre-structures in any universe).

*Proof.* Induction on the derivation. Axioms are valid by the two lemmas; premises vanish in a model of $\Gamma$; and if $\varphi=0$ and $\psi\dot-\varphi=0$ then $\psi\le\varphi=0$.

**Theorem** (`satisfiable_consistent_pre`, Theorem 7.2(ii)). A satisfiable $\Gamma$ is consistent.

*Proof.* The constant $1$ has value $1$ in the model, so by soundness it is not provable.

Introduction/TsubR.title: Truncated subtraction on the reals

paper.text: A truth assignment interprets the formal connective $\dot-$ as truncated subtraction of real numbers: the value of $\varphi\dot-\psi$ is the larger of $v(\varphi)-v(\psi)$ and $0$. Since $0$ means "true", $\psi\dot-\varphi$ vanishes exactly when the value of $\psi$ is at most that of $\varphi$, which is why the paper reads $\dot-$ as a kind of implication.

Introduction/TsubR.summary: Defines real truncated subtraction $x\dot-y=\max(x-y,0)$ with the infix notation `∸`, its iterate $b\dot-ka$, and the elementary inequalities about it that later soundness and evaluation proofs use (for example the real form of axiom (A2)).
Introduction/TsubR.english:
**Definition** (`tsubR`). For real numbers $x,y$ put $x\dot-y:=\max(x-y,0)$.

**Lemma** (basic facts). For all reals: $x\dot-y\ge0$; $x\dot-y=0$ iff $x\le y$; for $z\ge0$, $x\dot-y\le z$ iff $x-y\le z$ iff $x\le y+z$; $x\le y+(x\dot-y)$; and if $x\in[0,1]$, $y\ge0$ then $x\dot-y\in[0,1]$, while for $x,y\ge0$ we have $x\dot-y\le x$.

*Proof.* Each statement is a case distinction on whether $x\le y$, after unfolding the maximum; in each case the claim is a linear inequality.

**Lemma** (`tsub_tsub_le`, the real form of (A2)). For all $a,b,c$: $(c\dot-a)\dot-(c\dot-b)\le b\dot-a$.

*Proof.* Split on $c\le b$ and $c\le a$. If $c\le b$ then $c\dot-b=0$ and the left side is $c\dot-a$, which is $0$ when $c\le a$ and otherwise $c-a\le b-a$. If $c>b$ and $c\le a$ the left side is $0$. If $c>a$ and $c>b$ the left side is $\max((c-a)-(c-b),0)=b\dot-a$.

**Lemma.** For $x,y\ge0$: $x\dot-(x\dot-y)=\min(x,y)$. Also $(1-y)\dot-(1-x)=x\dot-y$ (negation reverses truncated subtraction), and $x\dot-x/2=x/2$ for $x\ge0$.

*Proof.* Case split on $x\le y$ for the minimum; the other two are direct computations of the difference inside the maximum.

**Definition** (`iterSubR`). $b\dot-0a:=b$ and $b\dot-(k+1)a:=(b\dot-ka)\dot-a$.

**Lemma** (`iterSubR_eq`). If $a,b\ge0$ then $b\dot-ka=\max(b-ka,0)$.

*Proof.* Induction on $k$. In the step, if $b\le ka$ both sides are $0$; otherwise $b-ka\ge0$ and subtracting $a$ once more gives $b-(k+1)a$ truncated at $0$.

**Lemma.** $x\dot-0=x$ for $x\ge0$.

Introduction/UnitInterval.title: Closure of the unit interval under negation and halving

paper.text: Truth values live in $[0,1]$: negation is interpreted as $x\mapsto 1-x$ and, in continuous logic, the extra connective $\tfrac12$ as $x\mapsto x/2$. Both maps send the unit interval into itself.

Introduction/UnitInterval.summary: Two one-line facts: $[0,1]$ is closed under $x\mapsto1-x$ and under $x\mapsto x/2$.
Introduction/UnitInterval.english:
**Lemma** (`unit_closed_neg`). If $0\le x\le1$ then $0\le1-x\le1$.

**Lemma** (`unit_closed_half`). If $0\le x\le1$ then $0\le x/2\le1$.

*Proof.* Both are linear inequalities that follow immediately from the hypotheses.

LanguageAndSemantics/CompletelySatisfiab.title: Complete satisfiability and entailment

paper.text: For a signature with a metric, $\Gamma$ is completely satisfiable if it has a model that is a genuine continuous structure (complete metric), and $\Gamma\models_{QC}\varphi$ if every such model of $\Gamma$ makes $\varphi$ zero.

LanguageAndSemantics/CompletelySatisfiab.summary: The variants of satisfiability and entailment that quantify only over complete continuous structures.
LanguageAndSemantics/CompletelySatisfiab.english: **Definition.** $\Gamma$ is completely satisfiable iff some continuous structure $\mathfrak M$ and assignment $\sigma$ satisfy $(\mathfrak M,\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$. $\Gamma\models_{QC}\varphi$ iff $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=0$ for every continuous structure and assignment that model $\Gamma$.

LanguageAndSemantics/ContinuousStructure.title: Continuous structures

paper.text: A continuous structure is a pre-structure in which $d$ is a genuine complete metric: distance $0$ forces equality, and Cauchy sequences converge.

LanguageAndSemantics/ContinuousStructure.summary: A metric pre-structure together with a metric-space structure on the carrier whose distance is $d^{\mathfrak M}$ and which is complete.
LanguageAndSemantics/ContinuousStructure.english: **Definition** (`ContinuousStructure`). A continuous $\mathcal L$-structure is a metric pre-structure $\mathfrak M$ together with a metric space structure on $M$ whose distance function equals $d^{\mathfrak M}$ and which is complete. Since a metric space separates points, $d^{\mathfrak M}(a,b)=0$ implies $a=b$.

LanguageAndSemantics/EntailsPre.title: Semantic entailment

paper.text: $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ means that $\varphi$ is $0$ in every model of $\Gamma$; a formula entailed by the empty set is valid.

LanguageAndSemantics/EntailsPre.summary: $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ over pre-structures and over metric pre-structures.
LanguageAndSemantics/EntailsPre.english: **Definition** (`EntailsPre`). $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ iff for every pre-structure $\mathfrak M$ (in universe $u$) and assignment $\sigma$ with $(\mathfrak M,\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$, $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=0$. `EntailsMetricPre` is the same with metric pre-structures.

LanguageAndSemantics/Formula.title: Formulae

paper.text: Formulae are built from atomic formulae $Pt_0\cdots t_{n-1}$ with the connectives $\dot-$, $\neg$, $\tfrac12$ and the quantifier $\sup_x$, as in classical first-order logic.

LanguageAndSemantics/Formula.english: **Definition** (`Formula`). The formulae of $\mathcal L$ are generated by: $P(t_0,\dots,t_{n_P-1})$ for a relation symbol $P$ and terms $t_i$; $\varphi\dot-\psi$; $\neg\varphi$; $\tfrac12\varphi$; and $\sup_x\varphi$ for a variable $x$. There is no separate $\inf$; it is defined in `FormulaConnectives`.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaConnectives.title: Derived connectives

paper.text:
Abbreviations: $\inf_x\varphi:=
eg\sup_x
eg\varphi$, $\varphi\wedge\psi:=\varphi\dot-(\varphi\dot-\psi)$, $\varphi\vee\psi:=
eg(
eg\varphi\wedge
eg\psi)$ and $|\varphi-\psi|:=(\varphi\dot-\psi)\vee(\psi\dot-\varphi)$. They are interpreted by infimum, minimum, maximum and absolute difference.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaConnectives.summary: $\inf$, $\wedge$, $\vee$, $|\cdot-\cdot|$, the truncated sum $\varphi\oplus\psi$ and the atomic formula $d(t_0,t_1)$.
LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaConnectives.english:
**Definitions.** $\inf_x\varphi:=
eg\sup_x
eg\varphi$; $\varphi\wedge\psi:=\varphi\dot-(\varphi\dot-\psi)$; $\varphi\vee\psi:=
eg(
eg\varphi\wedge
eg\psi)$; $|\varphi-\psi|:=(\varphi\dot-\psi)\vee(\psi\dot-\varphi)$; $\varphi\oplus\psi:=
eg(
eg\varphi\dot-\psi)$ (truncated addition); and for a metric signature, $d(t_0,t_1)$ is the metric symbol applied to $t_0,t_1$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaDefaultAtom.title: A fixed atomic formula

paper.text: The constant $1$ is written as $\neg(\varphi\dot-\varphi)$, which requires some formula $\varphi$ to exist; in first-order logic an atomic formula is always available because there is at least one relation symbol.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaDefaultAtom.summary: A canonical atomic formula $P(v_0,\dots,v_0)$, built from an arbitrarily chosen relation symbol, used to define the constant $1$.
LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaDefaultAtom.english: **Definition** (`defaultAtom`). Choose a relation symbol $P$ (possible since $\mathcal R\neq\emptyset$) and let $\varphi_0:=P(v_0,\dots,v_0)$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaDyadic.title: Dyadic constants as formulae

paper.text: Starting from $1$ and closing under the connectives one obtains formulae whose values are exactly the dyadic rationals in $[0,1]$; in particular $2^{-n}$ is $\tfrac12$ applied $n$ times to $1$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaDyadic.summary: The interpretation of dyadic codes as variable-free formulae, and the formula $2^{-n}$.
LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaDyadic.english:
**Definition** (`dyadic`). A dyadic code is turned into a formula by sending the code for $1$ to the formula $1$ and each code constructor to the corresponding connective $\neg$, $\dot-$, $\tfrac12$.

**Definition** (`pow2Neg`). $2^{-n}$ is the formula of the code for $2^{-n}$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaEquiv.title: Logical equivalence

paper.text: Two formulae are equivalent when they have the same value in every pre-structure under every assignment.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaEquiv.summary: $\varphi\equiv\psi$, both over all pre-structures and over metric pre-structures, and the implication between the two.
LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaEquiv.english:
**Definition.** $\varphi\equiv^f\psi$ iff $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=\mathfrak M(\psi,\sigma)$ for every pre-structure and assignment; $\varphi\equiv^m\psi$ is the same over metric pre-structures.

**Lemma.** $\varphi\equiv^f\psi$ implies $\varphi\equiv^m\psi$, because every metric pre-structure is a pre-structure.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaEval.title: The value of a formula

paper.text: The value $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)$ is defined by recursion: an atomic formula gets the value of its relation at the values of its terms; $\dot-$ is truncated subtraction, $\neg$ is $1-x$, $\tfrac12$ halves, and $\sup_x\alpha$ takes the supremum of the values of $\alpha$ over all reinterpretations of $x$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaEval.summary: $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)$ by recursion, its range $[0,1]$, and the values of the constants $1$ and of dyadic formulae.
LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaEval.english:
**Definition** (`Formula.eval`). $\mathfrak M(P\bar t,\sigma)=P^{\mathfrak M}(\bar t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma})$; $\mathfrak M(\alpha\dot-\beta,\sigma)=\mathfrak M(\alpha,\sigma)\dot-\mathfrak M(\beta,\sigma)$; $\mathfrak M(\neg\alpha,\sigma)=1-\mathfrak M(\alpha,\sigma)$; $\mathfrak M(\tfrac12\alpha,\sigma)=\mathfrak M(\alpha,\sigma)/2$; and $\mathfrak M(\sup_x\alpha,\sigma)=\sup_{a\in M}\mathfrak M(\alpha,\sigma^a_x)$.

**Lemma** (`eval_in_Icc`). Every value lies in $[0,1]$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$. Atomic values lie in $[0,1]$ by definition of a pre-structure; the three connectives preserve $[0,1]$. For $\sup_x\alpha$, the set of values is nonempty (since $M\neq\emptyset$) and bounded by $1$, so its supremum is at most $1$ and at least any member, hence at least $0$.

**Lemma.** The formula $1$ has value $1$, and the formula of a dyadic code $d$ has value $\mathrm{val}(d)$ under every assignment; hence the set of values of dyadic formulae is exactly the set of dyadic rationals in $[0,1]$ (Remark 3.4).

*Proof.* $\varphi_0\dot-\varphi_0$ has value $0$, so its negation has value $1$; the dyadic case is induction on the code.

paper.text: $\psi\dot-n\varphi$ abbreviates subtracting $\varphi$ from $\psi$ $n$ times in succession.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaOne.title: The constants 1 and 0

paper.text: Write $1$ for $\neg(\varphi\dot-\varphi)$ and $0$ for $\neg1$; their values are always $1$ and $0$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaOne.english: **Definition.** $1:=\neg(\varphi_0\dot-\varphi_0)$ and $0:=\neg1$, with $\varphi_0$ the default atom. (That $1$ has value $1$ is proved in `FormulaEval`.)

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaRank.title: Rank of a formula

paper.text: The rank counts connectives and quantifiers: atomic formulae have rank $0$, each unary connective or quantifier adds one, and $\varphi\dot-\psi$ has rank $\mathrm{rank}\,\varphi+\mathrm{rank}\,\psi+1$.

LanguageAndSemantics/FormulaRank.summary: The rank used for induction in the Henkin model theorem.

LanguageAndSemantics/MetricPreStructure.title: Pre-structures for a signature with a metric

paper.text: For a signature with a metric, $d$ must be interpreted as a pseudo-metric with values in $[0,1]$, and every symbol must respect its moduli: if $c$ and $e$ are closer than $\delta_{s,i}(\epsilon)$ then replacing $c$ by $e$ in argument $i$ moves a function value by at most $\epsilon$ in $d$, and increases a relation value by at most $\epsilon$.
These continuity requirements replace the congruence axioms for equality in classical logic; consequently every symbol is interpreted by a uniformly continuous map.

LanguageAndSemantics/MetricPreStructure.summary: Clauses (iii)–(v) of Definition 5.6: $d^{\mathfrak M}$ is a pseudo-metric, and functions and relations obey the moduli of the signature in each argument.

LanguageAndSemantics/MetricSignature.title: Signatures with a metric

paper.text: A signature with a metric singles out one binary relation symbol $d$. Unlike equality in classical logic, $d$ is a relation symbol, so $d\,t_0t_1$ is a formula with a truth value, not a term.

LanguageAndSemantics/MetricSignature.summary: A signature together with a distinguished relation symbol $d$ of arity $2$.
LanguageAndSemantics/MetricSignature.english: **Definition** (`MetricSignature`). A continuous signature with a metric is a continuous signature together with a relation symbol $d$ whose arity is $2$.

LanguageAndSemantics/ModelsPre.title: Models and satisfiability

paper.text: A pair of a pre-structure and an assignment is a model of $\Gamma$ when every formula of $\Gamma$ takes the value $0$ (which plays the role of "true"); $\Gamma$ is satisfiable when it has a model.

LanguageAndSemantics/ModelsPre.summary: $(\mathfrak M,\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$, satisfiability over all pre-structures in a universe, and over metric pre-structures.
LanguageAndSemantics/ModelsPre.english:
**Definition** (`ModelsPre`). $(\mathfrak M,\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$ iff $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\Gamma$.

**Definition.** $\Gamma$ is satisfiable (in universe $u$) iff some pre-structure in that universe and some assignment model it; for a signature with a metric, `SatisfiableMetricPre` requires a metric pre-structure.

LanguageAndSemantics/PreStructure.title: Pre-structures

paper.text: A continuous $\mathcal L$-pre-structure is a non-empty set $M$ in which every $n$-ary function symbol is interpreted by a map $M^n\to M$ and every $n$-ary relation symbol by a map $M^n\to[0,1]$.

LanguageAndSemantics/PreStructure.summary: Clauses (i)–(ii) of Definition 5.6: a nonempty carrier in an arbitrary universe, interpretations of function symbols, and $[0,1]$-valued interpretations of relation symbols.
LanguageAndSemantics/PreStructure.english: **Definition** (`PreStructure`). A pre-structure $\mathfrak M$ for $\mathcal L$ consists of a nonempty type $M$ (in an arbitrary universe $u$), for each function symbol $f$ a map $f^{\mathfrak M}:M^{n_f}\to M$, and for each relation symbol $P$ a map $P^{\mathfrak M}:M^{n_P}\to\mathbb R$ whose values lie in $[0,1]$.

LanguageAndSemantics/ReplaceArg.title: Replacing one argument of a tuple

paper.text: Conditions (iv) and (v) on pre-structures vary a single argument place: tuples $(\bar a,c,\bar b)$ and $(\bar a,e,\bar b)$ that agree except at position $i$.

LanguageAndSemantics/ReplaceArg.summary: The helper $v[i\mapsto c]$ used to state uniform continuity in one argument.
LanguageAndSemantics/ReplaceArg.english: **Definition** (`replaceArg`). For an $n$-tuple $v$, an index $i<n$ and an element $c$, $v[i\mapsto c]$ is the tuple whose $j$-th entry is $c$ if $j=i$ and $v_j$ otherwise. Thus $(\bar a,c,\bar b)$ with $|\bar a|=i$ is $v[i\mapsto c]$ for any $v$ extending $\bar a$ and $\bar b$.

LanguageAndSemantics/Signature.title: Continuous signatures

paper.text: A continuous signature consists of a non-empty set of relation symbols, a disjoint set of function symbols, an arity for every symbol, and for every symbol $s$ and argument place $i<n_s$ a modulus of uniform continuity $\delta_{s,i}:(0,1]\to(0,1]$.
The moduli are not symbols of the language; they are actual functions on $(0,1]$ that will constrain how the symbols may be interpreted.

LanguageAndSemantics/Signature.summary: A signature: types of relation and function symbols (relation symbols nonempty), arities, and real-valued moduli for each argument place mapping $(0,1]$ into $(0,1]$.
LanguageAndSemantics/Signature.english:
**Definition** (`Signature`). A continuous signature $\mathcal L$ consists of a type $\mathcal R$ of relation symbols, assumed nonempty, a type $\mathcal F$ of function symbols, arities $n_P$ and $n_f$, and for each symbol and argument index $i$ a function $\delta_{s,i}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that maps $(0,1]$ into $(0,1]$.

*Remark.* The moduli are total functions on $\mathbb R$ that are only constrained on $(0,1]$; this represents a function $(0,1]\to(0,1]$. Disjointness of $\mathcal R$ and $\mathcal F$ is automatic because they are separate types.

LanguageAndSemantics/Term.title: Terms

paper.text: Terms and formulae are built as in classical first-order logic; the paper does not spell out the grammar.

LanguageAndSemantics/Term.summary: Terms: variables and function symbols applied to tuples of terms.
LanguageAndSemantics/Term.english: **Definition** (`Term`). The terms of $\mathcal L$ are generated by two rules: every variable is a term, and if $f$ is a function symbol and $t_0,\dots,t_{n_f-1}$ are terms then $f(t_0,\dots,t_{n_f-1})$ is a term.

LanguageAndSemantics/TermEval.title: Interpretation of terms

paper.text: Terms are interpreted in a pre-structure under an assignment exactly as in classical logic.

LanguageAndSemantics/TermEval.english: **Definition** (`Term.eval`). Given a pre-structure $\mathfrak M$ and an assignment $\sigma:V\to M$: $x^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}=\sigma(x)$ and $f(t_0,\dots)^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}=f^{\mathfrak M}(t_0^{\mathfrak M,\sigma},\dots)$.

LanguageAndSemantics/UliftPreStructure.title: Lifting structures to larger universes

paper.text: The universe of a pre-structure is just a non-empty set; nothing in the paper depends on its size.

LanguageAndSemantics/UliftPreStructure.summary: Wrapping the carrier of a universe-$0$ (metric) pre-structure or continuous structure into a higher universe gives an isomorphic copy with the same truth values, so satisfiability in universe $0$ implies satisfiability in every universe.
LanguageAndSemantics/UliftPreStructure.english:
**Definition.** For a pre-structure $\mathfrak M$ in universe $0$, $\mathfrak M^\uparrow$ has carrier the lift of $M$ to universe $u$, with the symbols interpreted through the bijection $\mathrm{up}:M\to M^\uparrow$ and its inverse $\mathrm{down}$.

**Lemma.** For every term $t$ and formula $\varphi$: $t^{\mathfrak M^\uparrow,\mathrm{up}\circ\sigma}=\mathrm{up}(t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma})$ and $\mathfrak M^\uparrow(\varphi,\mathrm{up}\circ\sigma)=\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)$; equivalently $\mathfrak M^\uparrow(\varphi,\tau)=\mathfrak M(\varphi,\mathrm{down}\circ\tau)$.

*Proof.* Induction on $t$ and on $\varphi$. The only non-routine case is $\sup_x$: updating $\mathrm{up}\circ\sigma$ at $x$ with $\mathrm{up}(a)$ is $\mathrm{up}$ composed with $\sigma^a_x$, and $\mathrm{up}$ is a bijection, so both suprema range over the same set of values.

**Corollaries.** $(\mathfrak M^\uparrow,\mathrm{up}\circ\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$ iff $(\mathfrak M,\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$, so satisfiability in universe $0$ implies it in every universe. The same lifting works for metric pre-structures (the pseudo-metric axioms and moduli transfer through the bijection) and for continuous structures (the lifted metric is complete), so complete satisfiability also lifts.

LanguageAndSemantics/UpdateAssign.title: Updating an assignment

paper.text: An assignment maps variables into the structure; $\sigma^a_x$ is the assignment that sends $x$ to $a$ and agrees with $\sigma$ elsewhere.

LanguageAndSemantics/UpdateAssign.summary: The assignment $\sigma^a_x$ and its two evaluation rules.
LanguageAndSemantics/UpdateAssign.english:
**Definition** (`updateAssign`). $\sigma^a_x(y)=a$ if $y=x$ and $\sigma(y)$ otherwise.

**Lemma.** $\sigma^a_x(x)=a$, and $\sigma^a_x(y)=\sigma(y)$ for $y\neq x$.

LanguageAndSemantics/Var.title: Variables

paper.text: The logical symbols are parentheses, the connectives $\dot-$, $\neg$, $\tfrac12$, the quantifier $\sup$ (with $\inf$ as its dual), a countable list of variables $v_0,v_1,\dots$, and optionally a binary metric symbol $d$. The three connectives are the continuous analogue of the classical choice $\{\neg,\to\}$: finitely many, yet enough to approximate every continuous connective.

LanguageAndSemantics/Var.summary: Variables are natural numbers: $v_i$ is the number $i$.
LanguageAndSemantics/Var.english: **Definition** (`Var`). The set of variables is $V=\mathbb N$; the variable $v_i$ is represented by $i$. Equality of variables is decidable, and there are always fresh variables.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/AffineFn.title: Affine functions on real coordinate space
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/AffineFn.summary: Affine maps $x\mapsto c+\sum_i a_ix_i$ on $\mathbb R^n$ as data (coefficients and constant), with their algebra and the fact that they respect affine combinations and are continuous. These are the pieces of the piecewise-linear functions used in the semantic iteration lemma.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/AffineFn.english:
**Definition** (`AffineFn n`). An affine function is given by coefficients $a\in\mathbb R^n$ and a constant $c$; it evaluates to $c+\sum_i a_ix_i$. Constants, coordinate projections, sums, scalar multiples, negatives and differences of affine functions are affine, with the expected values.

**Lemma.** For an affine $a$, points $x,y$ and $t\in\mathbb R$: $a(x+t(y-x))=a(x)+t(a(y)-a(x))$, and $a((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)a(x)+ta(y)$; more generally $a(sx+ty)=sa(x)+ta(y)$ when $s+t=1$. Every affine function is continuous.

*Proof.* Expand the sum: the constant term is multiplied by $s+t=1$ and the linear part is linear. Continuity holds because a finite sum of continuous coordinate functions plus a constant is continuous.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLFromLuk.title: Continuous logic reduced to Łukasiewicz logic (proof of Fact 4.5)

paper.text: For finite premise sets continuous propositional logic is strongly complete: if finitely many premises semantically force $\varphi$, then $\varphi$ is derivable from them.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLFromLuk.summary: Treats each half-formula $\tfrac12\chi$ as a new propositional atom, so that continuous formulae become Łukasiewicz formulae; adding the finitely many relevant instances of (A5) and (A6) as premises forces the new atoms to take the value of $\tfrac12\chi$, and finite strong completeness for Łukasiewicz logic then yields Fact 4.5.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLFromLuk.english:
**Definitions.** `toLuk` reads a continuous formula as a Łukasiewicz formula over the variables $I\sqcup\{\text{continuous formulae}\}$, replacing each $\tfrac12\chi$ by the atom $[\chi]$; `ofLuk` substitutes back $\tfrac12\chi$ for $[\chi]$, and $\mathrm{ofLuk}(\mathrm{toLuk}\,\varphi)=\varphi$. Let $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ be the finite set of subformulae of $\varphi$ and $A_5(\chi)$, $A_6(\chi)$ the instances of (A5) and (A6) at $\chi$.

**Lemma** (`provable_ofLuk`). A Łukasiewicz proof from $S$ becomes, after substitution, a continuous-logic proof of $\mathrm{ofLuk}\,\varphi$ from $\mathrm{ofLuk}[S]$.

*Proof.* Induction on the proof: axioms (A1)–(A4) substitute to axioms, premises to premises, and modus ponens to modus ponens.

**Lemma** (`provable_cut`). If $S\vdash\varphi$ and every member of $S$ is provable from $T$, then $T\vdash\varphi$.

**Lemma** (`eval_toLuk`). Let $w$ be a $[0,1]$-assignment on the extended variables. If $w$ gives value $0$ to $\mathrm{toLuk}(A_5(\chi))$ and $\mathrm{toLuk}(A_6(\chi))$ for every $\tfrac12\chi$ occurring in $\psi$, then the Łukasiewicz value of $\mathrm{toLuk}\,\psi$ under $w$ equals the continuous value of $\psi$ under the restriction of $w$ to $I$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\psi$. The only nontrivial case is $\tfrac12\chi$: the two axiom instances say $w([\chi])\dot-(\chi\dot-w([\chi]))=0$ and $(\chi\dot-w([\chi]))\dot-w([\chi])=0$, which together force $w([\chi])=\chi/2$.

**Theorem** (`entails_finset_iff_provable`, Fact 4.5). For finite $\Sigma$: $\Sigma\models\varphi$ iff $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$.

*Proof.* Soundness gives one direction. For the other, let $C$ be the subformulae of $\varphi$ and of the members of $\Sigma$, $H$ the (A5)/(A6) instances for all $\tfrac12\chi\in C$, and $L=\mathrm{toLuk}[\Sigma\cup H]$, a finite set. Any $[0,1]$-assignment satisfying $L$ evaluates every relevant formula as in continuous logic, so it satisfies $\Sigma$ and hence gives $\mathrm{toLuk}\,\varphi$ the value $0$; thus $L\models\mathrm{toLuk}\,\varphi$. By finite strong completeness of Łukasiewicz logic $L\vdash\mathrm{toLuk}\,\varphi$; substituting back gives $\Sigma\cup H\vdash\varphi$ in continuous logic. Every member of $H$ is an axiom, so the cut lemma gives $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropForm.title: Formulae of continuous propositional logic

paper.text: Continuous propositional logic has the same propositional symbols, and its formulae are freely generated by $\dot-$, $\neg$ and one further unary connective $\tfrac12$ ("halving").

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropForm.summary: Continuous propositional formulae over a type $I$ of variables: the free term algebra generated by variables, $\dot-$, $\neg$ and $\tfrac12$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropForm.english: **Definition** (`CLPropForm I`). A formula is a variable $P_i$, a truncated difference $\varphi\dot-\psi$, a negation $\neg\varphi$, or a half $\tfrac12\varphi$. As for Łukasiewicz formulae the type is inductive, so formulae are freely generated and equality is decidable when it is decidable on $I$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormDeduc.title: Weak deduction theorem for continuous propositional logic

paper.text: The same weak deduction theorem holds in continuous propositional logic: a hypothesis can be discharged at the cost of subtracting it finitely many times from the conclusion.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormDeduc.summary: The same derived rules and weak deduction theorem as for Łukasiewicz logic, for continuous propositional formulae (the extra axioms (A5), (A6) are never needed in these derivations, only allowed).
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormDeduc.english:
**Notation.** Write $\varphi\to\psi$ for $\psi\dot-\varphi$ (so "$\to$" is provable exactly when the consequent is at most the antecedent), and $\varphi\vee\psi$ for $(\varphi\to\psi)\to\psi$.

**Lemma** (monotonicity, compactness). If $\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ then $\Gamma'\vdash\varphi$. If $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ then some finite $\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma$ proves $\varphi$.

*Proof.* Induction on derivations; for compactness, the finite set is the union of the finite sets of the premises of modus ponens.

**Lemma** (derived rules). The following are provable from any $\Gamma$, following Rose and Rosser: syllogism $(\varphi\to\psi)\to((\psi\to\chi)\to(\varphi\to\chi))$, which is (A2); $\varphi\to(\psi\vee\varphi)$ and $\varphi\to(\varphi\vee\psi)$; exchange of antecedents $(\varphi\to(\psi\to\chi))\to(\psi\to(\varphi\to\chi))$; reflexivity $\varphi\to\varphi$; prefixing $(\varphi\to\psi)\to((\chi\to\varphi)\to(\chi\to\psi))$; and congruence of $\dot-$ in its left argument, $(\varphi\to\psi)\to((\varphi\dot-\alpha)\to(\psi\dot-\alpha))$.

*Proof.* Each is a short chain of instances of (A1)–(A4) (the halving axioms are not needed) combined by modus ponens, transcribed from the Hilbert-style derivations of Rose and Rosser.

**Lemma** (iterated subtraction). (i) If $\vdash\varphi\to\psi$ and $\vdash\varphi\dot-n\alpha$ then $\vdash\psi\dot-n\alpha$. (ii) $\vdash(\beta\dot-\gamma)\dot-n\alpha\ \to\ (\beta\dot-n\alpha)\dot-\gamma$. (iii) $(\beta\dot-n\alpha)\dot-m\alpha$ is literally $\beta\dot-(n+m)\alpha$. (iv) From $\vdash(\beta\dot-\gamma)\dot-n\alpha$ and $\vdash\gamma\dot-m\alpha$ infer $\vdash\beta\dot-(n+m)\alpha$. (v) If $\Gamma\vdash\psi$ and $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-n\psi$ then $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$. (vi) The value of $\psi\dot-n\varphi$ is the real iterate $v(\psi)\dot-n\,v(\varphi)$.

*Proof.* (i) and (ii) by induction on $n$ using congruence and the commutation $((\beta\dot-\gamma)\dot-\alpha)\to((\beta\dot-\alpha)\dot-\gamma)$. (iii) by induction on $m$. (iv) combines (ii), (iii) and one modus ponens with $\gamma\dot-m\alpha$ moved to the front. (v) applies modus ponens $n$ times, peeling one copy of $\psi$ each time. (vi) by induction on $n$.

**Theorem** (`deduction_theorem`, weak deduction theorem). $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}\vdash\varphi$ if and only if $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-n\psi$ for some $n$.

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}$ proves both $\psi$ and $\varphi\dot-n\psi$, so it proves $\varphi$ by (v). ($\Rightarrow$) Induction on the derivation of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}$. Axioms and members of $\Gamma$ are proved from $\Gamma$ with $n=0$. The hypothesis $\psi$ itself gives $\psi\dot-1\psi=\psi\dot-\psi$, which is provable by reflexivity. If $\varphi$ was obtained by modus ponens from $\alpha$ and $\varphi\dot-\alpha$, the induction hypotheses give $\Gamma\vdash\alpha\dot-n\psi$ and $\Gamma\vdash(\varphi\dot-\alpha)\dot-m\psi$, and (iv) combines them into $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-(m+n)\psi$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormEval.title: Truth assignments for continuous propositional logic

paper.text: Truth assignments for continuous logic are computed exactly as for Łukasiewicz logic, with the additional clause that $\tfrac12\varphi$ receives half the value of $\varphi$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormEval.summary: The value of a continuous propositional formula under an assignment, by recursion, and its range $[0,1]$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormEval.english:
**Definition** (`CLPropForm.eval`). $v(P_i)=v_0(i)$, $v(\varphi\dot-\psi)=v(\varphi)\dot-v(\psi)$, $v(\neg\varphi)=1-v(\varphi)$ and $v(\tfrac12\varphi)=v(\varphi)/2$.

**Lemma** (`eval_mem_Icc`). If $v_0$ takes values in $[0,1]$, so does $v$.

*Proof.* Induction on the formula; the new case uses that $x/2\in[0,1]$ for $x\in[0,1]$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormModel.title: Models, satisfiability and entailment for continuous logic

paper.text: Models, satisfiable sets and semantic entailment for continuous propositional logic are defined word for word as in the Łukasiewicz case, now using the richer truth assignments.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormModel.summary: Models, satisfiability and semantic entailment for continuous propositional formulae.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormModel.english: **Definition.** An assignment $v_0:I\to[0,1]$ is a model of $\Sigma\subseteq$ `CLPropForm I` if every member of $\Sigma$ has value $0$; $\Sigma$ is satisfiable if it has a model; and $\Sigma\models\varphi$ if every model of $\Sigma$ gives $\varphi$ the value $0$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormSeman.title: Semantic iteration for continuous logic

paper.text: The same semantic iteration principle holds for continuous propositional logic with finitely many premises; it is the semantic half of the passage from Fact 4.5 for $\Sigma\cup\{\psi\}$ to Fact 4.5 for $\Sigma$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormSeman.summary: Semantic iteration for continuous formulae: halving is linear, so formulae are still piecewise linear and the same uniform bound applies.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormSeman.english:
**Definition.** `vars` $\varphi$ is the finite set of variables occurring in $\varphi$.

**Lemma** (`eval_eqOn`). Two assignments agreeing on the variables of $\varphi$ give $\varphi$ the same value.

**Definition.** For a finite set $s$ of variables, `restrictTo` sends an assignment to the vector of its values on $s$ (a point of $\mathbb R^{|s|}$), and `extendOn` turns a vector back into an assignment that is $0$ off $s$. Restricting a $[0,1]$-valued assignment lands in the cube, extending a point of the cube gives a $[0,1]$-valued assignment, and extending a restriction agrees with the original assignment on $s$, hence on every formula whose variables lie in $s$.

**Lemma** (`hasPL_eval`). If the variables of $\varphi$ lie in $s$, the function $x\mapsto v_x(\varphi)$ on $[0,1]^{|s|}$ is piecewise linear.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$, using closure of piecewise-linear functions under projections, $1-f$, truncated subtraction and multiplication by $\tfrac12$.

**Theorem** (`semantic_iteration`). Let $\Sigma$ be finite. If $\Sigma\cup\{\psi\}\models\varphi$ then there is $n$ with $\Sigma\models\varphi\dot-n\psi$.

*Proof.* Let $s$ collect the variables of $\Sigma$, $\varphi$ and $\psi$, and view every formula as a piecewise-linear function on the cube $[0,1]^{|s|}$. The hypothesis says exactly that $\varphi$ vanishes wherever all members of $\Sigma$ and $\psi$ vanish, and $\psi\ge0$. The cube lemma gives $N$ with $v(\varphi)\le N\,v(\psi)$ at every point where $\Sigma$ vanishes. Now take any model $v$ of $\Sigma$; its restriction to $s$ is such a point, so $v(\varphi)\le Nv(\psi)$, and therefore $v(\varphi\dot-N\psi)=\max(v(\varphi)-Nv(\psi),0)=0$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormSound.title: Soundness of continuous propositional logic

paper.text: Continuous propositional logic is sound for its truth assignments: provability from $\Sigma$ implies truth in all models of $\Sigma$, for arbitrary (also infinite) $\Sigma$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormSound.summary: Every axiom (A1)–(A6) evaluates to $0$, so $\Sigma\vdash^{\mathrm{CL}}\varphi$ implies $\Sigma\models^{\mathrm{CL}}\varphi$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/CLPropFormSound.english:
**Lemma** (`axiom_eval_zero`). Every instance of (A1)–(A6) evaluates to $0$.

*Proof.* (A1)–(A4) as in the Łukasiewicz case. For (A5) and (A6), with $a=v(\varphi)\ge0$ we have $a\dot-a/2=a/2$, so both $\tfrac a2\dot-(a\dot-\tfrac a2)$ and $(a\dot-\tfrac a2)\dot-\tfrac a2$ are $0$.

**Theorem** (`soundness`). If $\Sigma\vdash^{\mathrm{CL}}\varphi$ then $\Sigma\models^{\mathrm{CL}}\varphi$.

*Proof.* Induction on the derivation exactly as for Łukasiewicz logic: modus ponens preserves value $0$ since $v(\psi)\le v(\varphi)+v(\psi\dot-\varphi)$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/ChainGroup.title: The ordered abelian group of an MV-chain

paper.text: Chang's completeness proof represents every totally ordered MV-algebra as the interval $[0,u]$ of a linearly ordered abelian group; the paper cites this proof for Fact 4.1 rather than reproducing it.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/ChainGroup.summary: Chang's construction for an MV-chain $A$: pairs $(n,a)$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$, $a\in A\setminus\{1\}$ read as $n+a$ form a linearly ordered abelian group with strong unit $u=1+0$, into whose interval $[0,u]$ the chain embeds preserving $\ominus$ and $\neg$. Consequently a formula that is non-zero in a chain is non-zero in $[0,1]$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/ChainGroup.english:
Let $A$ be an MV-chain.

**Definition.** The *carry* of $a+b$ is $1$ if $a\oplus b=1$ and $0$ otherwise; the *fractional part* is $a\odot b$ in the first case and $a\oplus b$ in the second. The *digits* of $a+b+c$ are $(a\oplus b\oplus c,\ F(a,b,c),\ a\odot b\odot c)$, from which an integer part ($0$, $1$ or $2$) and a fractional part are read off.

**Lemma** (`fold_eq`). Adding $a$, $b$, $c$ from the left with carries yields the integer and fractional parts read off the digits; the digits are symmetric under all permutations of $a,b,c$.

*Proof.* Case analysis on $a\oplus b\oplus c=1$ and on $F(a,b,c)=1$, using the chain identities. Symmetry in the last two arguments is the theorem $F(x,y,z)=F(x,z,y)$; the other symmetries follow from commutativity.

**Definition** (`ChainGroup A`). Elements are pairs $(n,a)$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, $a\in A$, $a\ne1$, standing for "$n+a$". Addition is $(n,a)+(m,b)=(n+m+\mathrm{carry}(a,b),\ \mathrm{fsum}(a,b))$, zero is $(0,0)$, and the order is lexicographic.

**Theorem.** `ChainGroup A` is a linearly ordered abelian group.

*Proof.* Commutativity and the zero law are immediate; associativity follows from `fold_eq` because both bracketings compute the digits of $a+b+c$, which are symmetric. Negation of $(n,a)$ is $(-n,0)$ if $a=0$ and $(-n-1,\neg a)$ otherwise. The lexicographic order is linear because the MV-order on $A$ is, and it is translation invariant by a case analysis on carries.

**Definition** (`emb`). $u:=(1,0)>0$. Embed $A$ by $x\mapsto(0,x)$ for $x\ne1$ and $1\mapsto u$.

**Lemma.** The embedding is monotone, lands in $[0,u]$, sends only $0$ to $0$, is additive on sums without overflow ($a\odot b=0$), and satisfies $\mathrm{emb}(x\ominus y)=\max(\mathrm{emb}\,x-\mathrm{emb}\,y,0)$ and $\mathrm{emb}(\neg x)=u-\mathrm{emb}\,x$. Hence evaluating a formula in $[0,u]$ at $\mathrm{emb}\circ v$ gives the embedding of its MV-value at $v$.

**Theorem** (`exists_real_of_evalMV_chain_ne_zero`). If a Łukasiewicz formula has a non-zero value in an MV-chain, it has a non-zero value under some real $[0,1]$-assignment.

*Proof.* Its value in $[0,u]$ of the chain group is the embedding of a non-zero element, hence non-zero; now apply the transfer from ordered groups to $[0,1]$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/GroupEval.title: From the interval of an ordered group to the real unit interval
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/GroupEval.summary: Evaluates Łukasiewicz formulae in the interval $[0,u]$ of a linearly ordered abelian group ($\Gamma(G,u)$), and proves that a formula which is non-zero there is non-zero under some real $[0,1]$ assignment, by linearizing the formula around the given point and transferring the resulting inequalities to $\mathbb R$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/GroupEval.english:
**Definition** (`evalG`). For a linearly ordered abelian group $G$, an element $u>0$ and an assignment $a$ of variables in $[0,u]$, evaluate $\varphi\dot-\psi$ as $\max(\varphi-\psi,0)$ and $\neg\varphi$ as $u-\varphi$. Values stay in $[0,u]$.

**Definition** (linearization at a point). Fix a finite set $s$ of variables containing those of $\varphi$, and consider the vector $(u,a_i)_{i\in s}$. Following the branch actually taken at this point by each truncated subtraction, a formula is computed by an integer-linear form `lf` in $(u,a)$: a variable is its coordinate, $\neg\varphi$ is $u-\varphi$, and $\varphi\dot-\psi$ is $\varphi-\psi$ if $\psi\le\varphi$ at the point and $0$ otherwise. The *branch conditions* `cons` record, for each subtraction, the inequality ($\psi\le\varphi$, or $\varphi<\psi$) that selected the branch.

**Lemma.** At the point itself the linear form evaluates to the value of $\varphi$, and all branch conditions hold.

**Lemma** (`eval_realVal`). If a real vector $y$ with $y_u>0$ satisfies all branch conditions, then the real assignment $i\mapsto y_i/y_u$ gives $\varphi$ the value $\mathrm{lf}(y)/y_u$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$: the branch conditions guarantee that each truncated subtraction takes the same branch at the scaled real point.

**Theorem** (`exists_real_of_evalG_ne_zero`). If $\varphi$ has a non-zero value in $[0,u]$ of a linearly ordered abelian group, it has a non-zero value under some $[0,1]$-valued real assignment.

*Proof.* Collect the constraints $u>0$, $0\le a_i\le u$, all branch conditions of $\varphi$, and $\mathrm{lf}(\varphi)>0$. They hold at the point $(u,a)$ in $G$, so by the transfer theorem they have a real solution $y$. Then $y_u>0$, the assignment $y_i/y_u$ takes values in $[0,1]$, and the value of $\varphi$ there is $\mathrm{lf}(y)/y_u>0$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/HasPL.title: Piecewise-linear functions on the cube
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/HasPL.summary: A function on $[0,1]^n$ is piecewise linear if finitely many polyhedral cells cover the cube with an affine formula on each. Such functions are closed under constants, projections, $1-f$, scalar multiples and truncated subtraction, and they satisfy the uniform bound $f\le Ng$ used for semantic iteration.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/HasPL.english:
**Definition.** Cells can be intersected, cut by one more inequality $a\le0$, or cut to the hyperplane $a=0$; the whole cube is a cell. An *affine chart* is a cell with an affine function on it. A function $f$ is *piecewise linear* (`HasPL f`) if there is a finite list of charts whose cells cover $[0,1]^n$ and on each of which $f$ agrees with the chart's affine function.

**Lemma.** Constants and coordinate projections are piecewise linear (one chart, the cube). If $f$ is piecewise linear so are $1-f$ and $cf$.

**Lemma** (`HasPL.pair`, common refinement). For piecewise-linear $f,g$ there is one finite cover by cells on each of which both $f$ and $g$ are affine.

*Proof.* Intersect each cell of the first cover with each cell of the second.

**Lemma** (`hasPL_tsub`). If $f,g$ are piecewise linear, so is $x\mapsto f(x)\dot-g(x)$.

*Proof.* On a common refinement cell where $f=a$ and $g=b$ are affine, split the cell by the inequality $a-b\le0$: on that part $f\dot-g=0$, and on the part cut by $b-a\le0$ it equals $a-b$. The two parts cover the cell.

**Lemma** (`semantic_iteration_cube`). Let $h_1,\dots,h_k,f,g$ be piecewise linear on $[0,1]^n$ with $g\ge0$, and suppose that $f(x)=0$ at every point of the cube where all $h_j$ and $g$ vanish. Then there is $N$ with $f(x)\le Ng(x)$ at every point where all $h_j$ vanish.

*Proof.* Refine to finitely many cells on which $f$, $g$ and every $h_j$ are affine, and on each cell cut down to the set where all $h_j$ vanish (again a cell, by equalizing). On each such cell the hypotheses of the bounded-ratio lemma hold, giving an $N$ per cell; since the bound $f\le Ng$ is monotone in $N$, the maximum of these finitely many $N$ works everywhere.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LinearTransfer.title: Transfer of linear inequalities from ordered groups to the reals
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LinearTransfer.summary: Fourier–Motzkin elimination for finite systems of homogeneous integer-linear strict and non-strict inequalities: such a system with a solution in some linearly ordered abelian group also has a real solution.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LinearTransfer.english:
**Definition.** A constraint in $n$ variables is an integer vector $c$ and a flag; it says $0\le\sum_jc_jx_j$, or $0<\sum_jc_jx_j$ if the flag is set. It makes sense in any ordered abelian group.

**Definition** (Fourier–Motzkin step). Given a list of constraints in $n+1$ variables, keep those whose last coefficient is $0$ (dropping that variable), and for every pair $p$ with positive and $q$ with negative last coefficient add the combination $(-q_{n})\,p+p_n\,q$, whose last coefficient is $0$; it is strict if $p$ or $q$ is.

**Lemma** (`holds_elim`). If $x$ satisfies the system in an ordered abelian group, then the truncation of $x$ satisfies the eliminated system.

*Proof.* Positive integer multiples and sums of nonnegative (positive) elements are nonnegative (positive, if one summand is).

**Lemma** (`exists_between_lists`). Given finitely many real lower bounds $l_p$ and upper bounds $u_q$, each pair compatible (with strict inequality when either bound is strict), there is a real $t$ between all of them, respecting strictness.

*Proof.* Take $t$ between the maximum of the lower bounds and the minimum of the upper bounds, using the midpoint when some inequality must be strict.

**Theorem** (`exists_real_solution`, transfer). If a finite system of such constraints is solvable in a linearly ordered abelian group $G$, it is solvable in $\mathbb R$.

*Proof.* Induction on the number of variables. With no variables each constraint is a statement about $0$, which holds in $G$ iff it holds in $\mathbb R$. In the step, eliminate the last variable: the eliminated system holds at the truncated $G$-solution, so by induction it has a real solution $y'$. Each constraint with positive last coefficient gives a lower bound for the last coordinate in terms of $y'$, each with negative last coefficient an upper bound, and the eliminated combinations say precisely that every lower bound is below every upper bound. Choosing $t$ in between gives a real solution $(y',t)$; constraints not involving the last variable already hold at $y'$.

**Corollary** (`exists_real_solution_fintype`). The same holds for variables indexed by any finite type.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukChang.title: Chang's completeness theorem (proof of Fact 4.1)

paper.text: Weak completeness of Łukasiewicz logic: a formula is true under every truth assignment exactly when it is provable from the axioms alone.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukChang.summary: Assembles Chang's proof: an unprovable formula stays unprovable in some linear theory, whose Lindenbaum algebra is a chain in which the formula is non-zero, hence it is non-zero under some real assignment.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukChang.english:
**Theorem** (`provable_of_entails_empty`). If $\models\varphi$ then $\vdash\varphi$.

*Proof.* Suppose $
vdash\varphi$. Extend the empty premise set to a linear $\Delta$ with $\Delta
vdash\varphi$. The Lindenbaum algebra $\mathrm{Lind}(\Delta)$ is totally ordered, and $0
eq1$ there, since otherwise $[\varphi]\le1=0$ would give $\Delta\vdash\varphi$; so it is an MV-chain. At the canonical assignment $\varphi$ evaluates to $[\varphi]
eq0$. By the chain-group construction and the transfer to the reals, there is a $[0,1]$-valued assignment $w$ with $w(\varphi)
eq0$, contradicting $\models\varphi$.

**Theorem** (`entails_empty_iff_provable`). $\models\varphi$ iff $\vdash\varphi$. The other direction is soundness.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukFiniteStrong.title: Finite strong completeness for Łukasiewicz logic
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukFiniteStrong.summary: From weak completeness and the semantic and syntactic iteration (deduction) theorems: for a finite premise set $\Sigma$, $\Sigma\models\varphi$ implies $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukFiniteStrong.english:
**Theorem** (`provable_of_entails_finset`). If $\Sigma$ is a finite set of Łukasiewicz formulae and $\Sigma\models\varphi$, then $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\Sigma$, simultaneously for all $\varphi$. For $\Sigma=\emptyset$ this is weak completeness. If $\Sigma=\Sigma_0\cup\{\psi\}$ and $\Sigma\models\varphi$, the semantic iteration lemma gives $n$ with $\Sigma_0\models\varphi\dot-n\psi$; by induction $\Sigma_0\vdash\varphi\dot-n\psi$, and the deduction theorem turns this into $\Sigma_0\cup\{\psi\}\vdash\varphi$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukLindenbaum.title: The Lindenbaum algebra of Łukasiewicz logic

paper.text: The syntactic half of Chang's argument: modulo provable equivalence relative to a premise set, Łukasiewicz formulae form an MV-algebra in which a formula is provable exactly when its class is the zero element.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukLindenbaum.summary: Provable equivalence relative to $\Gamma$, the derived rules needed to make it a congruence (double negation, contraposition, exchange), the quotient $\mathrm{Lind}(\Gamma)$, and the proof that it is an MV-algebra in which $[\varphi]=0$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukLindenbaum.english:
Fix a set $\Gamma$ of Łukasiewicz formulae and write $\varphi\to\psi$ for $\psi\dot-\varphi$.

**Definition** (`ProvableEq`). $\varphi\equiv_\Gamma\psi$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\to\psi$ and $\Gamma\vdash\psi\to\varphi$. This is an equivalence relation; any two formulae provable from $\Gamma$ are equivalent; and $\varphi\equiv_\Gamma\psi\dot-\psi$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$.

*Proof.* Reflexivity and transitivity are the derived rules $\varphi\to\varphi$ and syllogism. Two theorems imply each other by (A1). For the last claim use that $\psi\dot-\psi$ is provable and that a formula equivalent to a theorem is a theorem by modus ponens.

**Lemma** (derived rules). Each is provable from any $\Gamma$: right antitonicity $(\alpha\to\beta)\to((\varphi\dot-\beta)\to(\varphi\dot-\alpha))$; axiom (A4) in implication form $(\neg\varphi\to\neg\psi)\to(\psi\to\varphi)$; ex falso $\neg\varphi\to(\varphi\to\psi)$; double negation $\neg\neg\varphi\to\varphi$ and $\varphi\to\neg\neg\varphi$; contraposition $(\varphi\to\psi)\to(\neg\psi\to\neg\varphi)$; and $\varphi\to(\psi\dot-\psi)$.

*Proof.* Short Hilbert-style derivations from (A1)–(A4), syllogism and exchange of antecedents; double negation elimination combines ex falso with (A4), and direct contraposition is obtained from the converse one by double negation.

**Lemma** (congruence). $\equiv_\Gamma$ is compatible with $\neg$ and with $\dot-$ in both arguments. Subtracting a theorem changes nothing, contraposition and exchange of antecedents are equivalences, and (A3) says that $\varphi\vee\psi\equiv\psi\vee\varphi$.

**Definition.** At the formula level $\varphi\oplus\psi:=\neg(\neg\varphi\dot-\psi)$. Up to $\equiv_\Gamma$ it is commutative and associative, has any theorem as neutral element and its negation as absorbing element, satisfies Chang's axiom, and $\varphi\dot-\psi\equiv\neg(\neg\varphi\oplus\psi)$.

*Proof.* Each identity reduces, by the congruence lemmas, to an equivalence between implications that is an instance of exchange, contraposition, double negation or (A3).

**Definition** (`LukLindT Γ`). The quotient of formulae by $\equiv_\Gamma$, with $\neg[\varphi]=[\neg\varphi]$, $[\varphi]\oplus[\psi]=[\varphi\oplus\psi]$ and $0=[\psi\dot-\psi]$ for any $\psi$ (all choices give the same class).

**Theorem** (`instMVAlgebra`). $\mathrm{Lind}(\Gamma)$ is an MV-algebra, its truncated subtraction is $[\varphi]\ominus[\psi]=[\varphi\dot-\psi]$, and $[\varphi]=0$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ (`mk_eq_zero_iff`).

**Theorem** (`provable_iff_evalMV_canonical`). Evaluating $\varphi$ in $\mathrm{Lind}(\Gamma)$ at the canonical assignment $i\mapsto[P_i]$ returns $[\varphi]$; hence $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ iff $\varphi$ evaluates to $0$ there.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$ using the descriptions of $\ominus$ and $\neg$ on classes.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukLinearTheory.title: Linear extensions and totally ordered Lindenbaum algebras

paper.text: In Chang's proof one passes from an arbitrary unprovable formula to a premise set under which any two formulae are comparable; its Lindenbaum algebra is then a chain.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukLinearTheory.summary: Order in the Lindenbaum algebra corresponds to provability of $\alpha\dot-\beta$; every premise set that does not prove $\varphi$ extends to a *linear* one (any two formulae comparable) that still does not prove $\varphi$; and the Lindenbaum algebra of a linear set is totally ordered.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukLinearTheory.english:
**Lemma.** In $\mathrm{Lind}(\Gamma)$: $[\varphi\dot-n\psi]=[\varphi]\ominus n[\psi]$, and $[\alpha]\le[\beta]$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\alpha\dot-\beta$.

**Definition** (`IsLinear`). $\Delta$ is linear if for all $\alpha,\beta$, $\Delta\vdash\alpha\dot-\beta$ or $\Delta\vdash\beta\dot-\alpha$.

**Theorem** (`exists_linear_extension`). If $\Gamma\nvdash\varphi$, there is a linear $\Delta\supseteq\Gamma$ with $\Delta\nvdash\varphi$.

*Proof.* The family of sets $\Delta\supseteq\Gamma$ with $\Delta\nvdash\varphi$ is closed under unions of nonempty chains, because a proof uses only finitely many premises and those lie in one member of the chain. By Zorn's lemma it has a maximal member $\Delta$. Suppose $\Delta$ proves neither $\alpha\dot-\beta$ nor $\beta\dot-\alpha$. By maximality, $\Delta\cup\{\alpha\dot-\beta\}\vdash\varphi$ and $\Delta\cup\{\beta\dot-\alpha\}\vdash\varphi$, and the weak deduction theorem gives $\Delta\vdash\varphi\dot-n(\alpha\dot-\beta)$ and $\Delta\vdash\varphi\dot-m(\beta\dot-\alpha)$. In $\mathrm{Lind}(\Delta)$, with $x=[\varphi]$, $p=[\alpha]\ominus[\beta]$, $q=[\beta]\ominus[\alpha]$, this says $x\le(n+m)p$ and $x\le(n+m)q$. By prelinearity $p\wedge q=0$, hence $(n+m)p\wedge(n+m)q=0$ and $x\le0$, i.e. $\Delta\vdash\varphi$, a contradiction.

**Lemma** (`le_total_of_isLinear`). If $\Delta$ is linear, the order of $\mathrm{Lind}(\Delta)$ is total.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropForm.title: Formulae of Łukasiewicz propositional logic

paper.text: Fix a set of distinct propositional symbols $P_i$, indexed by $i\in I$. A Łukasiewicz propositional logic is the set of formulae freely generated from these symbols by one binary connective $\dot-$ and one unary connective $\neg$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropForm.summary: Łukasiewicz formulae over a type $I$ of propositional variables, as the free term algebra generated by variables, $\dot-$ and $\neg$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropForm.english:
**Definition** (`LukPropForm I`). A formula is either a variable $P_i$ ($i\in I$), a truncated difference $\varphi\dot-\psi$ of two formulae, or a negation $\neg\varphi$. Because the type is inductive, formulae are freely generated: two formulae are equal only if they are built in the same way, and functions on formulae can be defined by recursion on this construction. Equality of formulae is decidable when it is decidable on $I$.

Note that there are no constant formulae: if $I$ is empty, the set of formulae is empty as well.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormDedu.title: Weak deduction theorem for Łukasiewicz logic

paper.text: The paper's deduction theorem (stated for continuous first-order logic, with the propositional case implicit in §4) says: adding a hypothesis $\psi$ lets us prove $\varphi$ exactly when, without it, we can prove $\varphi$ minus some finite number of copies of $\psi$. Its proof rests on a Łukasiewicz tautology that lets two such iterated subtractions be combined, followed by induction on the derivation.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormDedu.summary: The Hilbert-style toolkit for Łukasiewicz provability (monotonicity, compactness, syllogism, exchange, reflexivity, congruence, iterated subtraction) culminating in the weak deduction theorem $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}\vdash\varphi\iff\exists n,\ \Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-n\psi$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormDedu.english:
**Notation.** Write $\varphi\to\psi$ for $\psi\dot-\varphi$ (so "$\to$" is provable exactly when the consequent is at most the antecedent), and $\varphi\vee\psi$ for $(\varphi\to\psi)\to\psi$.

**Lemma** (monotonicity, compactness). If $\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma'$ and $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ then $\Gamma'\vdash\varphi$. If $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ then some finite $\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma$ proves $\varphi$.

*Proof.* Induction on derivations; for compactness, the finite set is the union of the finite sets of the premises of modus ponens.

**Lemma** (derived rules). The following are provable from any $\Gamma$, following Rose and Rosser: syllogism $(\varphi\to\psi)\to((\psi\to\chi)\to(\varphi\to\chi))$, which is (A2); $\varphi\to(\psi\vee\varphi)$ and $\varphi\to(\varphi\vee\psi)$; exchange of antecedents $(\varphi\to(\psi\to\chi))\to(\psi\to(\varphi\to\chi))$; reflexivity $\varphi\to\varphi$; prefixing $(\varphi\to\psi)\to((\chi\to\varphi)\to(\chi\to\psi))$; and congruence of $\dot-$ in its left argument, $(\varphi\to\psi)\to((\varphi\dot-\alpha)\to(\psi\dot-\alpha))$.

*Proof.* Each is a short chain of instances of (A1)–(A4) combined by modus ponens, transcribed from the Hilbert-style derivations of Rose and Rosser.

**Lemma** (iterated subtraction). (i) If $\vdash\varphi\to\psi$ and $\vdash\varphi\dot-n\alpha$ then $\vdash\psi\dot-n\alpha$. (ii) $\vdash(\beta\dot-\gamma)\dot-n\alpha\ \to\ (\beta\dot-n\alpha)\dot-\gamma$. (iii) $(\beta\dot-n\alpha)\dot-m\alpha$ is literally $\beta\dot-(n+m)\alpha$. (iv) From $\vdash(\beta\dot-\gamma)\dot-n\alpha$ and $\vdash\gamma\dot-m\alpha$ infer $\vdash\beta\dot-(n+m)\alpha$. (v) If $\Gamma\vdash\psi$ and $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-n\psi$ then $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$. (vi) The value of $\psi\dot-n\varphi$ is the real iterate $v(\psi)\dot-n\,v(\varphi)$.

*Proof.* (i) and (ii) by induction on $n$ using congruence and the commutation $((\beta\dot-\gamma)\dot-\alpha)\to((\beta\dot-\alpha)\dot-\gamma)$. (iii) by induction on $m$. (iv) combines (ii), (iii) and one modus ponens with $\gamma\dot-m\alpha$ moved to the front. (v) applies modus ponens $n$ times, peeling one copy of $\psi$ each time. (vi) by induction on $n$.

**Theorem** (`deduction_theorem`, weak deduction theorem). $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}\vdash\varphi$ if and only if $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-n\psi$ for some $n$.

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}$ proves both $\psi$ and $\varphi\dot-n\psi$, so it proves $\varphi$ by (v). ($\Rightarrow$) Induction on the derivation of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma\cup\{\psi\}$. Axioms and members of $\Gamma$ are proved from $\Gamma$ with $n=0$. The hypothesis $\psi$ itself gives $\psi\dot-1\psi=\psi\dot-\psi$, which is provable by reflexivity. If $\varphi$ was obtained by modus ponens from $\alpha$ and $\varphi\dot-\alpha$, the induction hypotheses give $\Gamma\vdash\alpha\dot-n\psi$ and $\Gamma\vdash(\varphi\dot-\alpha)\dot-m\psi$, and (iv) combines them into $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-(m+n)\psi$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormEval.title: Truth assignments for Łukasiewicz logic

paper.text: A map $v_0$ from the propositional symbols to $[0,1]$ extends uniquely to all formulae: the value of $\varphi\dot-\psi$ is the truncated difference of the values, and the value of $\neg\varphi$ is one minus the value of $\varphi$. This extension is the truth assignment determined by $v_0$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormEval.summary: The value of a Łukasiewicz formula under an assignment $v_0:I\to\mathbb R$, defined by recursion, and the fact that it lies in $[0,1]$ whenever $v_0$ does.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormEval.english:
**Definition** (`LukPropForm.eval`). Given $v_0:I\to\mathbb R$, define $v(P_i)=v_0(i)$, $v(\varphi\dot-\psi)=v(\varphi)\dot-v(\psi)$ and $v(\neg\varphi)=1-v(\varphi)$.

**Lemma** (`eval_mem_Icc`). If $v_0(i)\in[0,1]$ for every $i$, then $v(\varphi)\in[0,1]$ for every formula $\varphi$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$. Variables hold by hypothesis; a truncated difference of a value in $[0,1]$ and a nonnegative value lies in $[0,1]$; and $1-x\in[0,1]$ when $x\in[0,1]$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormMode.title: Models, satisfiability and entailment for Łukasiewicz logic

paper.text: An assignment is a model of a set $\Sigma$ of formulae when it gives every member of $\Sigma$ the value $0$ (truth). $\Sigma$ is satisfiable when it has a model, and $\Sigma$ semantically entails $\varphi$ when every model of $\Sigma$ is also a model of $\varphi$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormMode.summary: Models, satisfiability and semantic entailment $\Sigma\models\varphi$ for Łukasiewicz formulae, with assignments ranging over $[0,1]$-valued maps.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormMode.english:
**Definition** (`Models`). An assignment $v_0:I\to\mathbb R$ is a model of $\Sigma$ if every $v_0(i)$ lies in $[0,1]$ and $v(\varphi)=0$ for every $\varphi\in\Sigma$.

**Definition** (`Satisfiable`). $\Sigma$ is satisfiable if it has a model.

**Definition** (`Entails`). $\Sigma\models\varphi$ if every model of $\Sigma$ gives $\varphi$ the value $0$.

The range condition $v_0(i)\in[0,1]$ is part of being a model, so assignments are exactly the maps of the paper into the unit interval.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormSema.title: Semantic iteration for Łukasiewicz logic

paper.text: Finite strong completeness relies on a semantic counterpart of the deduction theorem: for a finite set of premises, if $\psi$ together with $\Sigma$ forces $\varphi$ to be true, then already $\Sigma$ forces $\varphi$ minus some fixed multiple of $\psi$ to be true. With finitely many premises one bound works for all models; the infinite example $\{P\dot-2^{-n}\}$ in the paper shows this fails in general.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormSema.summary: For finitely many premises, $\Sigma\cup\{\psi\}\models\varphi$ implies $\Sigma\models\varphi\dot-n\psi$ for one $n$, proved by viewing formulae as piecewise-linear functions on a cube.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormSema.english:
**Definition.** `vars` $\varphi$ is the finite set of variables occurring in $\varphi$.

**Lemma** (`eval_eqOn`). Two assignments agreeing on the variables of $\varphi$ give $\varphi$ the same value.

**Definition.** For a finite set $s$ of variables, `restrictTo` sends an assignment to the vector of its values on $s$ (a point of $\mathbb R^{|s|}$), and `extendOn` turns a vector back into an assignment that is $0$ off $s$. Restricting a $[0,1]$-valued assignment lands in the cube, extending a point of the cube gives a $[0,1]$-valued assignment, and extending a restriction agrees with the original assignment on $s$, hence on every formula whose variables lie in $s$.

**Lemma** (`hasPL_eval`). If the variables of $\varphi$ lie in $s$, the function $x\mapsto v_x(\varphi)$ on $[0,1]^{|s|}$ is piecewise linear.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$, using closure of piecewise-linear functions under projections, $1-f$, truncated subtraction (and halving, for continuous formulae).

**Theorem** (`semantic_iteration`). Let $\Sigma$ be finite. If $\Sigma\cup\{\psi\}\models\varphi$ then there is $n$ with $\Sigma\models\varphi\dot-n\psi$.

*Proof.* Let $s$ collect the variables of $\Sigma$, $\varphi$ and $\psi$, and view every formula as a piecewise-linear function on the cube $[0,1]^{|s|}$. The hypothesis says exactly that $\varphi$ vanishes wherever all members of $\Sigma$ and $\psi$ vanish, and $\psi\ge0$. The cube lemma gives $N$ with $v(\varphi)\le N\,v(\psi)$ at every point where $\Sigma$ vanishes. Now take any model $v$ of $\Sigma$; its restriction to $s$ is such a point, so $v(\varphi)\le Nv(\psi)$, and therefore $v(\varphi\dot-N\psi)=\max(v(\varphi)-Nv(\psi),0)=0$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormSoun.title: Soundness of Łukasiewicz propositional logic

paper.text: The paper notes that both propositional proof systems are sound: whatever is provable from $\Sigma$ is true in every model of $\Sigma$. This is the easy direction of the completeness facts.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormSoun.summary: Every axiom (A1)–(A4) evaluates to $0$, and therefore $\Sigma\vdash^{\mathrm L}\varphi$ implies $\Sigma\models^{\mathrm L}\varphi$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/LukPropFormSoun.english:
**Lemma** (`axiom_eval_zero`). Every instance of (A1)–(A4) has value $0$ under every $[0,1]$-valued assignment.

*Proof.* Write $a,b,c$ for the values of $\varphi,\psi,\chi$. (A1) says $(a\dot-b)\dot-a=0$, true because $a\dot-b\le a$ for $a,b\ge0$. (A2) is the real inequality $(c\dot-a)\dot-(c\dot-b)\le b\dot-a$. (A3) holds because both $a\dot-(a\dot-b)$ and $b\dot-(b\dot-a)$ equal $\min(a,b)$. (A4) holds because $(1-b)\dot-(1-a)=a\dot-b$.

**Theorem** (`soundness`). If $\Sigma\vdash\varphi$ then $\Sigma\models\varphi$.

*Proof.* Induction on the derivation. Axioms have value $0$ by the lemma, and hypotheses have value $0$ in every model of $\Sigma$. For modus ponens, if a model gives $\varphi$ and $\psi\dot-\varphi$ the value $0$, then $v(\psi)\le v(\varphi)=0$, so $v(\psi)=0$ because values are nonnegative.
