Otherwise $x\odot y\odot z=0$ and we split on whether $x\oplus y$ and $x\oplus z$ equal $1$: if both do, the key identity $(x\odot y)\oplus z=(x\odot z)\oplus y$ (proved by a longer computation with cancellation) finishes; if exactly one does, the mixed identity above finishes; if neither does, dualize.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/PolyCell.title: Polyhedral cells in the unit cube and bounded ratios
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/PolyCell.summary: Polyhedral cells (the unit cube cut by finitely many affine inequalities), their compactness and convexity, finiteness of their extreme points, attainment of affine maxima at extreme points, and the key estimate: if $g\ge0$ and $f$ vanishes wherever $g$ does on a cell, then $f\le Ng$ there for some integer $N$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/PolyCell.english:
**Definition.** The unit cube $[0,1]^n$; it is compact and convex, and it is described by the $2n$ affine inequalities $x_i-1\le0$, $-x_i\le0$. A *polyhedral cell* is the set of points of the cube satisfying finitely many further affine inequalities $a(x)\le0$. Cells are closed, compact and convex subsets of the cube.

**Lemma** (`tightSet_injOn_extremePoints`, `finite_extremePoints`). Distinct extreme points of a cell satisfy different sets of constraints with equality. Hence a cell has finitely many extreme points.

*Proof.* Suppose two distinct extreme points $x\neq y$ have the same tight constraints. Every constraint not tight at $x$ or at $y$ is strict there, so for small $\varepsilon>0$ the points $x\pm\varepsilon(y-x)$ still satisfy all constraints (tight ones stay tight by affinity, strict ones stay strict by continuity). Then $x$ is the midpoint of two distinct points of the cell, contradicting extremality. Since there are finitely many sets of constraints, there are finitely many extreme points.

**Lemma** (`exists_extreme_isMaxOn`). On a nonempty cell every affine function attains its maximum at an extreme point.

*Proof.* The cell is compact, so the maximum is attained; the set of maximizers is a nonempty compact face, and by the Krein–Milman theorem it has an extreme point, which is extreme in the whole cell.

**Lemma** (`affine_ratio_bound`). Let $f,g$ be affine, $g\ge0$ on a cell $C$, and suppose $f(x)=0$ whenever $x\in C$ and $g(x)=0$. Then there is $N\in\mathbb N$ with $f\le Ng$ on $C$.

*Proof.* If $C$ is empty take $N=0$. Otherwise let $N$ be the maximum, over the finitely many extreme points $x$ with $g(x)>0$, of $\lceil f(x)/g(x)\rceil$. Then $f-Ng\le0$ at every extreme point (at those with $g=0$ we have $f=0$). The affine function $f-Ng$ attains its maximum on $C$ at an extreme point, so it is $\le0$ on all of $C$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/PropCompactness.title: Compactness, consistency and approximated completeness (proofs of Facts 4.2–4.4)

paper.text: For Łukasiewicz logic a set of formulae is consistent precisely when some truth assignment satisfies it.
The same equivalence of consistency and satisfiability holds for continuous propositional logic.

Approximated strong completeness: $\Sigma$ semantically implies $\varphi$ exactly when $\Sigma$ proves $\varphi\dot-2^{-n}$ for every $n$; in other words entailment is the limit of provable approximations, without requiring $\Sigma$ to prove $\varphi$ itself.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/PropCompactness.summary: Compactness of $[0,1]^I$ (Tychonoff) and continuity of evaluation give propositional compactness; combined with finite strong completeness this proves Facts 4.2 and 4.3 (with the added premise that there is at least one propositional variable, and with a counterexample when there is none) and Fact 4.4.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/PropCompactness.english:
**Lemma** (`exists_common_zero`). If continuous functions $f_j:[0,1]^I\to\mathbb R$ have a common zero in the cube on every finite subfamily, they have a common zero in the cube.

*Proof.* The cube is compact by Tychonoff, and the zero sets are closed sets with the finite intersection property.

**Lemma.** For a Łukasiewicz or continuous formula, $v\mapsto v(\varphi)$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^I$, since $\dot-$, $1-x$ and $x/2$ are continuous.

**Theorem** (`satisfiable_of_finite`, compactness). A set of formulae is satisfiable if each finite subset is.

**Theorem** (`satisfiable_of_consistent`). For any $I$, a consistent $\Gamma$ is satisfiable (Łukasiewicz and continuous versions).

*Proof.* If not, compactness gives a finite unsatisfiable $\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma$. Then $\Gamma_0\models\varphi$ vacuously for every $\varphi$, so by finite strong completeness $\Gamma_0\vdash\varphi$ and hence $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$ for every $\varphi$: $\Gamma$ is inconsistent.

**Theorem** (`consistent_of_satisfiable`). If there is at least one propositional variable $P$, a satisfiable $\Gamma$ is consistent.

*Proof.* Let $v$ satisfy $\Gamma$. The formula $\neg(P\dot-P)$ has value $1$ under $v$, so by soundness it is not provable from $\Gamma$.

**Theorem** (`consistent_iff_satisfiable`, Facts 4.2 and 4.3). If $I$ is nonempty, $\Gamma$ is consistent iff it is satisfiable.

**Theorem** (`consistent_iff_satisfiable_fails_empty`). With no propositional variables there are no formulae; then $\emptyset$ is satisfiable but, vacuously, inconsistent, so the equivalence fails as literally stated.

**Theorem** (`entails_iff_forall_provable_tsub_pow2Neg`, Fact 4.4). $\Gamma\models\varphi$ iff $\Gamma\vdash\varphi\dot-2^{-n}$ for all $n$, where the constant $2^{-n}$ is the dyadic formula built from $\varphi$.

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) By soundness every model has $v(\varphi)\le2^{-n}$ for all $n$, hence $v(\varphi)=0$. ($\Rightarrow$) Fix $n$. The conditions "every premise is $0$" and "$2^{-n}\dot-\varphi=0$" (i.e. $\varphi\ge2^{-n}$) have no common zero, since a common zero would be a model of $\Gamma$ with $\varphi\ne0$. By the compactness lemma some finite subfamily already has no common zero; let $\Gamma_0$ be the premises occurring in it. Then $\Gamma_0\models\varphi\dot-2^{-n}$, finite strong completeness gives $\Gamma_0\vdash\varphi\dot-2^{-n}$, and monotonicity gives the claim for $\Gamma$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/StandardMVAlgeb.title: The standard MV-algebra on the unit interval

paper.text: The intended semantics evaluates formulae in $[0,1]$ with $\dot-$ as truncated subtraction and $\neg$ as $1-x$. In algebraic terms this is the standard MV-algebra on the unit interval, with $x\oplus y=\min(x+y,1)$.

LukasiewiczAndContinuous/StandardMVAlgeb.summary: The unit interval with $x\oplus y=\min(x+y,1)$ and $\neg x=1-x$ is an MV-algebra; evaluation of Łukasiewicz formulae in any MV-algebra; on the standard algebra it agrees with the real-valued truth assignments, so $\models\varphi$ means $\varphi$ evaluates to $0$ in $[0,1]$.
LukasiewiczAndContinuous/StandardMVAlgeb.english:
**Definition** (`unitIAdd`). On $[0,1]$ put $x\oplus y:=\min(x+y,1)$.

**Lemma.** With $\neg x=1-x$: $\neg(\neg x\oplus y)=x\dot-y$; $\oplus$ is associative; and $(x\ominus y)\oplus y=\max(x,y)$.

*Proof.* Each is a case analysis on which of the minima and maxima are attained, reducing to linear arithmetic.

**Theorem** (`unitInterval.instMVAlgebra`). $([0,1],\oplus,\neg,0)$ is an MV-algebra.

*Proof.* Associativity and commutativity were shown above, $x\oplus0=x$, $1-(1-x)=x$, $x\oplus1=1$, and Chang's axiom holds because both sides equal $\max(x,y)$.

**Definition** (`evalMV`). For an assignment $v$ of variables in an MV-algebra $A$, evaluate $\varphi\dot-\psi$ as $v(\varphi)\ominus v(\psi)$ and $\neg\varphi$ as $\neg v(\varphi)$.

**Lemma** (`evalMV_coe`). On the standard algebra, MV-evaluation is the paper's real-valued truth assignment.

*Proof.* Induction on the formula, using $\neg(\neg x\oplus y)=x\dot-y$ and $\neg x=1-x$.

**Lemma** (`entails_empty_iff_evalMV`). $\models\varphi$ (no premises) iff $\varphi$ evaluates to $0$ under every assignment into the standard MV-algebra.

*Proof.* Real assignments with values in $[0,1]$ and assignments into the standard algebra correspond to each other (`liftVal`), and the two evaluations agree.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/BoundSubstitu.title: The Bound Substitution Lemma

paper.text: Given finitely many variables, a formula can be transformed by bound renamings into an equivalent formula in which none of them is bound. The paper calls this immediate and refers to classical textbooks.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/BoundSubstitu.summary: Renaming a bound variable to a variable absent from the formula preserves the value; iterating over a finite set of variables yields Lemma 6.4, for plain and for metric equivalence.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/BoundSubstitu.english:
**Definition** (`freshAbove`). For a finite set $s$ of variables, $\mathrm{fresh}(s)$ is a variable larger than every member of $s$, hence not in $s$.

**Lemma.** $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\subseteq\mathrm{AV}(\varphi)$; free substitution does not change bound variables; substituting a variable $y\notin\mathrm{AV}(\varphi)$ is always correct, and so is any substitution for a variable not free in $\varphi$.

**Lemma** (`eval_boundSubst`). If $y\notin\mathrm{AV}(\varphi)$ then $\mathfrak M(\varphi\{y/x\},\sigma)=\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)$ for all $\mathfrak M,\sigma$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$. At $\sup_x\alpha$ the result is $\sup_y\alpha'[y/x]$; by the Substitution Lemma (correct because $y$ is fresh) the value at $\sigma^b_y$ is the value of $\alpha'$ at $(\sigma^b_y)^b_x$, which by coincidence ($y$ not free in $\alpha'$) is the value of $\alpha'$ at $\sigma^b_x$; and $\alpha'$ has the value of $\alpha$ by induction.

**Lemma.** If $y\ne x$ then $x\notin\mathrm{BV}(\varphi\{y/x\})$, and $\mathrm{BV}(\varphi\{y/x\})\subseteq\mathrm{BV}(\varphi)\cup\{y\}$.

**Definition** (`BoundSubstReach`). $\varphi'$ is reachable from $\varphi$ if it arises by a finite (possibly empty) sequence of bound substitutions.

**Theorem** (`bound_substitution_lemma`, Lemma 6.4). For variables $x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}$ there is $\varphi'$ reachable from $\varphi$ in which no $x_i$ is bound and $\varphi\equiv\varphi'$; likewise for metric equivalence.

*Proof.* Induction on the finite set $s=\{x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}\}$. For $s\cup\{a\}$, take $\varphi_1$ for $s$ and a variable $y$ above $s\cup\{a\}\cup\mathrm{AV}(\varphi_1)$, and put $\varphi'=\varphi_1\{y/a\}$. Then $a$ is no longer bound, the new bound variable $y$ is not in $s$, the members of $s$ remain unbound, and $\varphi'$ has the same value as $\varphi_1$, hence as $\varphi$. Metric equivalence follows from plain equivalence.

A separate renaming function `renameBound` (renaming every clashing binder to a fresh variable in one pass) is also shown to preserve values and to avoid a given set.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/ElementaryLMo.title: Elementary L-morphisms

paper.text: An elementary morphism is a morphism that preserves the truth value of every formula under every assignment.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/ElementaryLMo.summary: Elementary morphisms as morphisms with value preservation.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/ElementaryLMo.english: **Definition** (`ElementaryLMorphism`). An $\mathcal L$-morphism $h$ such that $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=\mathfrak N(\varphi,h\circ\sigma)$ for every formula $\varphi$ and every assignment $\sigma$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/EntailsMetric.title: Entailment over complete structures

paper.text: For signatures with a metric, nothing changes if one restricts to complete structures: entailment over pre-structures equals entailment over complete structures, and satisfiability equals complete satisfiability.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/EntailsMetric.summary: Corollary 6.11: entailment and satisfiability over metric pre-structures coincide with their versions over complete (continuous) structures, by passing to the metric completion along an elementary morphism.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/EntailsMetric.english:
**Theorem** (`entails_metric_iff_complete`). $\Gamma\models_Q\varphi$ over metric pre-structures iff $\Gamma\models_{QC}\varphi$.

*Proof.* A continuous structure is a metric pre-structure, which gives one direction. Conversely let $(\mathfrak M,\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$ and let $h:\mathfrak M\to\widehat{\mathfrak M}$ be elementary. Then $(\widehat{\mathfrak M},h\circ\sigma)\models_Q\Gamma$ because values are preserved, so $\widehat{\mathfrak M}(\varphi,h\circ\sigma)=0$, and therefore $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=0$.

**Theorem** (`satisfiable_metric_iff_complete`). $\Gamma$ is satisfiable in a metric pre-structure iff it is completely satisfiable.

*Proof.* Push a model forward along the elementary morphism into its completion; the converse is trivial.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/EvalUniformly.title: Uniform continuity of definable maps

paper.text: If the variables of a term $t$ (the free variables of a formula $\varphi$) are among $x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}$, then $t$ and $\varphi$ induce maps $M^n\to M$ and $M^n\to[0,1]$ by assigning $a_i$ to $x_i$.
These induced maps are uniformly continuous; the paper's proof is an induction that combines the moduli of the symbols as in Remark 5.8.
From the one-argument moduli one obtains a modulus for all arguments at once, e.g. $\Delta_f(\epsilon)=\min_i\delta_{f,i}(\epsilon/n_f)$, measured in the maximum distance on tuples.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/EvalUniformly.summary: Definition 6.7 and Theorem 6.8 for metric pre-structures: symbols are jointly uniformly continuous (Remark 5.8), and so are term and formula evaluation as functions of the assignment, in the variables that occur.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/EvalUniformly.english:
Let $\mathfrak M$ be a metric pre-structure and $D(\bar a,\bar b)=\max_id(a_i,b_i)$.

**Definition** (`tildeTerm`, `tildeFormula`). For distinct variables $\bar x$ and $\bar a\in M^n$, $\tilde t(\bar a)$ and $\tilde\varphi(\bar a)$ are the values of $t$ and $\varphi$ under an assignment with $x_i\mapsto a_i$ (arbitrary elsewhere). If the relevant variables are among $\bar x$, these values do not depend on the choice elsewhere.

**Lemma** (Remark 5.8). For every function symbol $f$ and $\epsilon\in(0,1]$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $D(\bar u,\bar v)<\delta$ implies $d(f\bar u,f\bar v)\le\epsilon$; similarly, for a relation symbol, $|P\bar u-P\bar v|\le\epsilon$.

*Proof.* Change one argument at a time: with $\delta=\min_i\delta_{f,i}(\epsilon/n)$, each step moves the value by at most $\epsilon/n$, and the triangle inequality bounds the total. For relations, the modulus bounds the truncated difference in each direction, hence the absolute difference.

**Lemma.** $|(a\dot-b)-(c\dot-d)|\le|a-c|+|b-d|$, and if two bounded families of reals differ pointwise by at most $\epsilon$, so do their suprema.

**Lemma** (`term_eval_unif_cont`, `formula_eval_unif_cont`). For every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that any two assignments that are $\delta$-close on the variables of $t$ (resp. the free variables of $\varphi$) give $\epsilon$-close values.

*Proof.* Induction. Terms: compose the joint modulus of $f$ with the moduli of the arguments. Formulae: atomic as for terms; $\dot-$ splits $\epsilon$ between the two sides; $\neg$ and $\tfrac12$ do not increase distances; for $\sup_x\alpha$ use the same $\delta$ as for $\alpha$, since updating both assignments at $x$ with the same element keeps them $\delta$-close on $\mathrm{FV}(\alpha)$, and suprema of pointwise $\epsilon$-close families are $\epsilon$-close.

**Theorem** (`eval_uniformly_continuous`, Theorem 6.8). The maps $\tilde t:M^n\to M$ and $\tilde\varphi:M^n\to[0,1]$ are uniformly continuous with respect to $D$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/ExistsMetricC.title: Existence of metric completions

paper.text: Each pre-structure for a signature with a metric admits an elementary morphism into a continuous structure, its metric completion.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/ExistsMetricC.english:
**Theorem** (`exists_metric_completion`, Theorem 6.9). For every metric pre-structure $\mathfrak M$ (in universe $u$) there is a continuous structure $\widehat{\mathfrak M}$ in the same universe and an elementary $\mathcal L$-morphism $\mathfrak M\to\widehat{\mathfrak M}$.

*Proof.* Take the metric completion and its canonical elementary morphism.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaBoundS.title: Bound substitution

paper.text: $\varphi\{y/x\}$ renames the bound variable $x$ to $y$: each subformula $\sup_x\alpha$ becomes $\sup_y\alpha[y/x]$. The renaming is correct when $y$ is not free in $\alpha$ and the inner substitution is correct.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaBoundS.english:
**Definition** (`boundSubst`). $\varphi\{y/x\}$ fixes atomic formulae, commutes with connectives, sends $\sup_x\alpha$ to $\sup_y(\alpha'[y/x])$ and $\sup_z\alpha$ ($z\ne x$) to $\sup_z\alpha'$, where $\alpha'=\alpha\{y/x\}$.

**Definition** (`BoundSubstCorrect`). Correct if at every subformula $\sup_x\alpha$, $y\notin\mathrm{FV}(\alpha)$ and $\alpha[y/x]$ is correct, and recursively in all subformulae.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaFreeSu.title: Free substitution

paper.text: $\varphi[t/x]$ replaces the free occurrences of $x$ in $\varphi$ by $t$; it is correct when no variable of $t$ becomes bound by a quantifier in the result.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaFreeSu.english:
**Definition** (`freeSubst`). $\varphi[t/x]$ substitutes $t$ for $x$ in the terms of atomic formulae, commutes with the connectives, leaves $\sup_x\alpha$ unchanged, and for $y\neq x$ sends $\sup_y\alpha$ to $\sup_y(\alpha[t/x])$.

**Definition** (`FreeSubstCorrect`). The substitution is correct if, for every subformula $\sup_y\alpha$ with $y\neq x$ through which it passes, either $x$ is not free in $\alpha$ or $y$ does not occur in $t$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaFreeVa.title: Free, bound and all variables; sup-closure
SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaFreeVa.summary: Free, bound and all variables of a formula, and the sup-closure $\sup_{x_1}\cdots\sup_{x_k}\varphi$ that binds all free variables.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaFreeVa.english:
**Definitions.** $\mathrm{FV}(P\bar t)=\bigcup\mathrm{vars}(t_i)$, connectives take unions, and $\mathrm{FV}(\sup_x\alpha)=\mathrm{FV}(\alpha)\setminus\{x\}$. $\mathrm{BV}$ collects the variables bound by some $\sup$, and $\mathrm{AV}$ all variables occurring at all.

**Definition** (`supClosure`). List the free variables of $\varphi$ in increasing order $x_1<\dots<x_k$ and put $\overline\varphi:=\sup_{x_1}\cdots\sup_{x_k}\varphi$.

**Lemma.** $\overline\varphi$ has no free variables, and $\overline\varphi=\varphi$ when $\varphi$ is already a sentence.

*Proof.* Prefixing $\sup_{x}$ for each $x$ in a list removes exactly those variables from the free variables.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaHasFun.title: Occurrences of a constant; replacing it by a variable

paper.text: If a constant symbol not occurring in $\Gamma$ appears in a provable formula, it may be replaced by a variable, and the result is again provable.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaHasFun.summary: Whether a function symbol occurs in a term or formula, and $\varphi[x/c]$.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/FormulaHasFun.english: **Definitions.** $c$ occurs in $t$ if $t$ is an application of $c$ or $c$ occurs in an argument; it occurs in $\varphi$ if it occurs in some term of $\varphi$. $\varphi[x/c]$ replaces every occurrence of the constant $c$ in the terms of $\varphi$ by the variable $x$ (quantifiers are left unchanged).

SubstitutionAndCompletions/LMorphism.title: L-morphisms; surjective morphisms are elementary

paper.text: An $\mathcal L$-morphism commutes with the function symbols and preserves the values of the relation symbols exactly; it is elementary if it preserves the value of every formula under every assignment. With a metric symbol, every morphism is therefore an isometry.
A surjective $\mathcal L$-morphism is automatically elementary, by induction on formulae.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/LMorphism.summary: Morphisms of pre-structures (Definition 6.5) and Theorem 6.6: a surjective morphism preserves the value of every formula under every assignment.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/LMorphism.english:
**Definition** (`LMorphism`). A map $h:M\to N$ with $h(f^{\mathfrak M}(\bar a))=f^{\mathfrak N}(h\bar a)$ and $P^{\mathfrak M}(\bar a)=P^{\mathfrak N}(h\bar a)$.

**Lemma** (`map_term`). $h(t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma})=t^{\mathfrak N,h\circ\sigma}$, by induction on $t$.

**Theorem** (`surjective_morphism_elementary`, Theorem 6.6). If $h$ is surjective then $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=\mathfrak N(\varphi,h\circ\sigma)$ for all $\varphi,\sigma$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$. Atomic formulae use `map_term` and preservation of relations; the connectives are immediate. For $\sup_x\alpha$: $h\circ\sigma^a_x=(h\circ\sigma)^{h(a)}_x$, so by induction the values on the left are the values $\mathfrak N(\alpha,(h\circ\sigma)^{h(a)}_x)$, $a\in M$; by surjectivity these are all the values $\mathfrak N(\alpha,(h\circ\sigma)^b_x)$, $b\in N$. The suprema of equal sets are equal.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/MetricPreStru.title: The metric completion of a pre-structure

paper.text: Every pre-structure for a metric signature maps elementarily into a complete continuous structure for the same signature. The key fact is that a map with a modulus of uniform continuity, defined on a subset of a metric space and valued in a complete space, extends uniquely to the closure with the same modulus; so the moduli of the signature survive the completion.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/MetricPreStru.summary: Constructs $\widehat{\mathfrak M}$: the carrier is the metric completion of $(M,d^{\mathfrak M})$, symbols are extended by uniform continuity, the extensions keep their moduli, $d$ extends to the metric of the completion, and the inclusion is an elementary morphism.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/MetricPreStru.english:
**Definition.** $(M,d^{\mathfrak M})$ is a pseudo-metric space; let $\hat M$ be its completion and $\iota:M\to\hat M$ the canonical map.

**Lemma.** $f^{\mathfrak M}$ and $P^{\mathfrak M}$ are uniformly continuous on $M^n$ (from the joint moduli). Hence they have unique uniformly continuous extensions $\hat f:\hat M^n\to\hat M$ and $\hat P:\hat M^n\to\mathbb R$ with $\hat f(\iota\bar a)=\iota f(\bar a)$ and $\hat P(\iota\bar a)=P(\bar a)$, using that $\hat M^n$ is the completion of $M^n$.

**Lemma.** $\hat P$ takes values in $[0,1]$; the extended metric symbol $\hat d$ coincides with the metric of $\hat M$; and $\hat f,\hat P$ satisfy the same one-argument moduli $\delta_{s,i}$ as $f,P$.

*Proof.* Each property is a closed condition that holds on the dense image of $M$ and is preserved under limits. For the moduli: if $d(c,e)<\delta(\epsilon)$ in $\hat M$, approximate $c,e$ and the other arguments by points of $M$ that are still $\delta(\epsilon)$-close (possible because the inequality is strict); the modulus inequality holds for the approximants and passes to the limit by continuity.

**Definition** (`metricCompletion`). $\widehat{\mathfrak M}=(\hat M,\hat f,\hat P)$ is a continuous $\mathcal L$-structure: $\hat d$ is the complete metric of $\hat M$, and the moduli hold.

**Lemma.** $\iota$ is an $\mathcal L$-morphism with dense image.

**Lemma.** If a real function $g$ on a space is continuous with values in $[0,1]$ and $S$ is dense, then $\sup g[S]=\sup g$.

**Theorem** (`metricCompletionElementary`). $\iota$ is elementary: $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)=\widehat{\mathfrak M}(\varphi,\iota\circ\sigma)$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$; atomic formulae and connectives are as for morphisms. For $\sup_x\alpha$: the map $b\mapsto\widehat{\mathfrak M}(\alpha,(\iota\circ\sigma)^b_x)$ is continuous on $\hat M$ (by Theorem 6.8 applied in $\widehat{\mathfrak M}$), its values at $b=\iota(a)$ are $\mathfrak M(\alpha,\sigma^a_x)$ by induction, and $\iota[M]$ is dense; so the supremum over $\hat M$ equals the supremum over $M$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/PiCompletion.title: Completion of finite products
SubstitutionAndCompletions/PiCompletion.summary: For a pseudo-metric space $\alpha$, the $n$-fold product of its completion, with the componentwise inclusion, is a completion of $\alpha^n$; this is what lets $n$-ary symbols be extended to the completion.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/PiCompletion.english:
**Definition** (`piCoe`). The componentwise inclusion $\alpha^n\to\hat\alpha^n$.

**Lemma.** It is an isometry for the sup-metric and has dense range.

*Proof.* Distances are computed coordinatewise; density holds because a finite product of dense subsets is dense in the product.

**Definition** (`finPiCompletion`). Hence $\hat\alpha^n$, with `piCoe`, satisfies the universal property of the completion of $\alpha^n$: it is complete, Hausdorff, and contains a dense uniform-embedded copy of $\alpha^n$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/SubstitutionL.title: The Substitution Lemma

paper.text: If $\varphi[t/x]$ is a correct substitution, then evaluating it under $\sigma$ is the same as evaluating $\varphi$ under the assignment that sends $x$ to the value of $t$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/SubstitutionL.summary: Lemma 6.2, together with the coincidence lemmas: evaluation depends only on the (free) variables actually present.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/SubstitutionL.english:
**Lemma.** If $x\ne y$ then $(\sigma^a_y)^v_x=(\sigma^v_x)^a_y$.

**Lemma** (term substitution). $(s[t/x])^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}=s^{\mathfrak M,\sigma^a_x}$ with $a=t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}$.

**Lemma** (coincidence). If $y\notin\mathrm{vars}(t)$ then $t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma^a_y}=t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}$; if $x\notin\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$ then $\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma^a_x)=\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma)$.

*Proof.* Induction on $t$, resp. $\varphi$; in the case $\sup_z\alpha$ with $z\ne x$, swap the updates at $x$ and $z$ and use the induction hypothesis pointwise inside the supremum, while for $z=x$ the outer update is overwritten.

**Theorem** (`substitution_lemma`, Lemma 6.2). If $\varphi[t/x]$ is correct, then $\mathfrak M(\varphi[t/x],\sigma)=\mathfrak M(\varphi,\sigma^a_x)$ with $a=t^{\mathfrak M,\sigma}$.

*Proof.* Induction on $\varphi$, for all $\sigma$. Atomic formulae: the term lemma. Connectives: immediate. For $\sup_x\alpha$ the substitution does nothing, and $x$ is not free, so the coincidence lemma applies. For $\sup_y\alpha$ with $y\ne x$: if $x\notin\mathrm{FV}(\alpha)$ the substitution is invisible semantically and both sides equal $\mathfrak M(\sup_y\alpha,\sigma)$ by coincidence. Otherwise correctness gives $y\notin\mathrm{vars}(t)$, so $t$ has the same value $a$ under every $\sigma^b_y$; applying the induction hypothesis at $\sigma^b_y$ and commuting the updates shows that the families whose suprema are taken coincide.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/TermSubst.title: Substitution in terms

paper.text: The proof of Lemma 8.4 replaces a new constant symbol by a variable throughout a derivation.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/TermSubst.summary: $s[t/x]$ for terms, and replacement of a constant symbol by a variable.
SubstitutionAndCompletions/TermSubst.english: **Definitions.** $s[t/x]$ replaces every occurrence of $x$ in $s$ by $t$. For a $0$-ary function symbol $c$, $s[x/c]$ replaces every occurrence of the constant $c$ by the variable $x$.

SubstitutionAndCompletions/TermVars.title: Variables of a term
SubstitutionAndCompletions/TermVars.summary: The finite set of variables occurring in a term.
